Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors, the HDE model using the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within cyclic cosmology. Furthermore, we discovered that cyclic patterns of contraction and expansion may occur for both interacting and non-interacting universes, provided that the Granda-Oliveros cutoff is selected for the HDE's energy density.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix, for which an alternative proof has been devised. Furthermore, the former result for directed graphs has a corresponding update, for which its hermitian version yields the bond scattering matrix of undirected graphs.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its order-4 conjugacy class.

In experiments at Belle and Belle II, algorithms employed to search for rare or displacement-based decays of B mesons are complementary in their approach. We propose using machine learning methods to identify the invisible decays of B mesons into displaced ones, thereby expanding the sensitivity of the Belle II experiment to an intermediate mass range of axial vector particles (around a GeV) where current constraints from Belle are relatively loose. With projected data from Belle II, this strategy is expected to achieve S~1 sensitivity in this area, significantly outperforming what can be achieved with the existing data (S~0.1).

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies that
can arise from employing contextualized language models in identifying semantic
shifts in language. Our analysis led us to identify key factors that influence
the capabilities of contextualized encoders, specifically the contextual
aggregation method and the degree of context sensitivity required to accurately
capture semantic transformations. Additionally, we observed a significant
relationship between these elements and contextualized models' performance in
identifying semantic changes, ultimately resulting in a contextualized
semantic change detection (CSCD) benchmark.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) that have been observed to rotate at high speeds have been found to possess negligible spin due to ultralight boson-induced spin suppression. This phenomenon occurs when heavy quasars absorb a specific range of ultralight bosons, particularly those matching the mass of a heavy quasar's spectrum, which can deplete the cloud of bosons and leave the quasar with a high spin. As a result, active galactic nuclei produced by such "spin-friendly" ULBs would exhibit distinct characteristics compared to traditional models. Furthermore, it has been found that an active galactic nucleus produced by a "spin-unfriendly" boson would have a more symmetric light curve due to a symmetric distribution of bosons in a heavy quasar's spacetime. This unique property could be used to identify active galactic nuclei that are generated by heavy quasars that have high spins and those that are generated by lighter quasars.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we are the first to apply foraging theory
to understand how migrating nuclei make decisions about their direction. Our analysis
of zebrafish retina development using live imaging and software tools for tracking and
data processing has led to several key findings about nuclear behavior. We observed
that the average time it takes for a nucleus to complete a full migration cycle is
consistent across all nuclei, despite them taking different paths. We also observed
that the speed of nuclear movement varies based on the distance of the nucleus from the
upper layer, likely as an adaptive response to optimize growth. Our simulations
demonstrated that this strategy of velocity adjustment can be explained as a nucleus
attempting to reach an upper energy state, and we propose that a nucleus' decision-making
process can be understood through maximum entropy methods based on observed behaviors.
Our research also reveals that the optimal migration time is influenced by the properties
of the tissue's upper and lower layers, and we provide an estimate for the optimal
migration time that the system as a whole would experience.

In various image processing tasks, such as demosaicing and compressive video reconstruction, obtaining a clean and accurate result from a corrupted or incomplete input relies heavily on separating the missing information from the known information. This paper presents a unified approach to encode both types of data in a way that maximizes their separability, using a technique called linear unmixing. Through testing on complete demosaicing and demosaicing under compressed sensing, our encoding method outperforms existing techniques, achieving better mean squared error and visual quality metrics on standard demosaicing benchmarks.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

The evolution of scholarly articles forms a specialized network that is driven by academic collaborations, and these collaborations can be seen as interconnected relationships between researchers evolving over time. Researchers within this field employ a combination of Zhihu and TensorFlow frameworks to analyze the network of scholars, using a subset of the CNKI database as a sample. From 1999 to 2018, they examined the development of papers, articles, and collaborators across ten distinct disciplines. Notably, higher-degree researchers are more likely to have their work cited, whereas those in the periphery of the network often experiment with new topics, whereas central researchers tend to focus on established topics. Furthermore, power-law distribution is more commonly observed in highly interconnected central collaborations, whereas near-linear distribution is found in isolated peripheral collaborations.

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of "exceptional" van Hove singularities, where a fragment 
of a Fermi surface exerts a strong influence, disproportionate to its size, 
on the material's collective behavior. We argue that small, singularity- 
possessing electron pockets, responsible for charge density waves, 
Luttinger liquids, and superconductivity, embody this notion best. We then 
apply this idea to study electron interactions within a two-dimensional 
square lattice, subject to a weak magnetic field, and observe that 
singularity- 
possessing electron pockets appear at specific points as they merge, 
and that orientation of this singularity is crucial in this context.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built to investigate the effects of spallation neutrons in the Aberdeen Tunnel spallation lab, located in the Aberdeen Laboratory for Underground Research in Scotland. The lab's unique environment, characterized by high levels of natural gamma radiation and spallation neutrons, has been modified with the apparatus to allow for the study of neutron effects in more detail. Unfortunately, access to the lab has been restricted since accidents in 2019 prevented full access to the tunnel, limiting the available data to surface levels of gamma radiation. Consequently, the apparatus is also suitable for use in other underground laboratories around the world that offer access to their tunnels.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements within the TESS sectors can be accomplished using the TRES, HIRES, and MIRCIII instruments, which are compatible with TESS's wavelength range and offer high-precision measurements using TRES and HIRES, as well as astrometric measurements with MIRCIII. The primary goal of these follow-up observations is to detect the presence of exoplanets through TESS's transit and TRES/HIRES radial velocity measurements, while MIRCIII will sense the presence of small planets through its astrometric movements. The optimal strategy for each case is to use TRES/HIRES for larger ones and MIRCIRC for smaller ones, although the best approach for each may differ. The best strategy for each case is to allocate TESS time and MIRCIRC or TRES/HIRES observations to maximize the likelihood of detecting planets using TESS and the ground-based instruments, although this is complicated by the fact that we do not yet know the typical distribution of planetary sizes. The typical approach for each case is to allocate TESS time and MIRCIRC or TRES/HIRES observations to maximize the likelihood of detecting small planets using TESS and the ground-based instruments, although this is complicated by the fact that we do not yet know the typical distribution of small ones. The typical approach for each case is to allocate TESS time and MIRCIRC or TRES/HIRES observations to a sample of TESS targets, although this is complicated

This paper introduces a solution to automate the extraction of information from Indonesian identity cards, a crucial step in streamlining Indonesian government digitalization plans. Manually extracting this data is an inevitable part of the process, but it can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. To optimize this process, the proposed solution utilizes optical character recognition (OCR) in conjunction with natural language processing to parse and parse the extracted text. This approach allows for more efficient and accurate data collection, a critical step in improving government service delivery in Indonesia.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect has a significant impact on the rotation of celestial bodies in the solar system, particularly non-spherical asteroids that experience net forces and torques resulting from the uneven emission of absorbed solar radiation. In order to identify rotation acceleration or deceleration caused by this effect, a thorough analysis was performed on photometric light curves of asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, utilizing historical data spanning several decades. The findings revealed distinct changes in the spin periods of these asteroids, with the rate of change in Geographos being the most pronounced among them. The magnitude of the YORP torques experienced by the asteroids was found to be in the range of $10^{4}$ to $10^{5}$ N m.

The youth on social media platforms engage in political discussions that can
significantly impact their political development. To better understand this
phenomenon from a network perspective, our research focuses on a subset of
Instagram users who posted about key global events in 2019, specifically the
COVID-19 pandemic, the #MeToo movement, and the Black Lives Matter protests.
By analyzing the co-occurrence networks formed by these users and their
discussions, we aim to explore how these youth interact and connect with one
another. An examination of community structures within these networks, along
with an astheticetic assessment, enables us to track their evolution over
time. A comparative analysis of user engagement with different types of
content, as well as an exploration of user interactions and influences, are
also part of our investigation. Furthermore, we look at the content users
share and how they connect with one another in an effort to track the
propagation of specific topics within the network.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Precise stellar characteristics are vital for comprehending stellar evolution and the development of planetary systems. Many studies focusing on exoplanets orbiting M-dwarfs lack detailed information about their host stars. This project aims to provide a comprehensive set of stellar characteristics for a sample of 79 M-dwarf stars with M-plansets, by utilizing existing data from various sources. A systematic approach was employed to derive a set of stellar parameters, encompassing effective temperature, surface gravity, radius, rotation period, and surface metallicity. Validation of the obtained parameters was conducted using a sample of 27 M-dwarf stars in binary systems. This study found that 74% of the stars in the sample rotate at a slow pace, indicating a higher likelihood of habitability for any potential rocky planets in their circumstellar zones. Furthermore, this study found that 74% of the stars in the sample are devoid of spots in their ultraviolet spectra, indicating a higher likelihood of stable planetary conditions. This M-dwarf sample is considered a prime location for the search for habitable planets, utilizing existing data from various sources, including optical spectra, near-infrared spectra, and X-ray spectra.

Confining lines to the corner of a surface and directing their curvature enables a phenomenon known as line waves, which has so far been restricted to two dimensions. Digital optical metasurfaces transform two-dimensional light patterns into real images, yet confining line waves has only been observed in the unit square without applications in digital light processing. In this research, a novel two-dimensional meta-device incorporating a single curved line wave region is designed. This device effectively confines and directs line waves into a curvature of 0.5 lines per unit, enabling precise control and focusing. The devised meta-device exhibits improved efficiency in line wave focusing when illuminated by plane waves in the ultraviolet spectrum. Furthermore, the curable line waves focused by this device can be used to draw intricate curved patterns on a two-dimensional surface using ultraviolet light.

Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification is well-established for various types of queries, self-joined queries remain unclassified. This research aims to bridge this gap by examining the complexity of evaluating queries with self-joins. We present complexity classifications for both decision and enumeration problems, considering different output requirements such as read-only and reportable answers. Notably, our analysis reveals that self-joins can actually simplify complexity in certain cases, leading to novel results including APX-hard and NPO-complete findings.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, some of these transducers produce non-regular function outputs, which restrict their use in composing with other relations without losing a specific compositional logic property known as the modular verification of programs. We identify and explain a precise set of criteria that a function must meet to guarantee that it has a computable implementation using MSdO regular transducers for all d ≥ 1, and this is further discussed in the context of Computation Tree Logic and first-order logic with successive coordinates.

Researchers have analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment, which contained 3.0 inverse femtobarns of $bb$ collisions, to study the behavior of certain subatomic particles known as $B^0$, $B^0_s$, and $B^+$, specifically how they transform into pairs of $K^{*0}$ particles. By utilizing an technique called the amplitude method, they were able to measure the likelihood of $B^0$ transforming into $K^{*0}\overline{K}^{*0}$ and $\overline{K}^{*0}K^{*0}$, both of which came out to be 0.54±0.08(stat)±0.06(sys), allowing them to calculate the likelihood of $B^0$ transforming into $K^{*0}\overline{K}^{*0}$ as 0.30±0.08±0.06, with similar but slightly differing outcomes for $B^+$ and $B^0_s$.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems, including those with multiple coexisting states of attraction. Although previous methods have successfully trained on systems with a single, known attractor, they fall short when it comes to entities with attractors that don't exist physically. This research presents a novel approach for a reservoir computing reservoir to learn and generalize patterns associated with an attractor, even one that doesn't exist. By utilizing a pre-trained reservoir and a limited amount of data representing two distinct external influences, the model can accurately predict an attractor that has not been directly observed. When evaluated on a Preissler model, the reservoir computing reservoir demonstrated exceptional accuracy in this prediction, using 99.9% less data than would be required to train on the attractor alone.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears useful in the broader application of mixed Gaussian processes.  The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through an application and comparative analysis using simulation.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints in complex systems, a variance-reduced Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation solver is proposed. This proposal builds upon a Hamiltonian framework by incorporating a stochastic approximation of the reachability matrix, which is crucial for knowing all possible states reachable from a starting point. An innovative approach is introduced to estimate this information efficiently. An iterative process is developed that directly links past and future points in a sequence to gradually improve the optimality of the controller and state transitions. This process is proved to converge to the best possible solution under certain conditions. An underlying fixed-point relation is identified and used to explain the process's convergence. An underlying Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation is characterised by a unique solution that represents the minimum distance from the target set. An innovative approach is introduced to solve this characterisation, which is essential for the process's success.

Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) have been previously utilized in specific applications,
such as robotic control, where they have been effective in specific tasks.
However, their application in other fields has been limited due to their
high sensitivity to data that reflects prior information. This makes them
impractical for generating data that accurately represents specific functions
without explicit training. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to
functional approximation based on periodically activated, modulated MLP
blocks. This approach enables precise estimation of target functions using a
relatively small number of neural network units. By incorporating stochastic
elements and an expectation operator, we ensure that our network produces
periodically activated, modulated units that ensure its output is an accurate
representation of the target function. An algorithm has been developed to
create an optimal arrangement of activation and modulation patterns within
the network. This allows for precise estimation of complex functions such as
periodic functions and functions with multiple variables. An important
advantage of this approach is its ability to accurately represent a target
function with an error rate of only 0.01, solely based on network structure,
thus ensuring the approach is fully generalizable.

The brain's intricate neural networks have adapted to efficiently process recurring and evolutionarily significant stimuli, including those that differentiate living things from inanimate objects. Animacy discrimination, once thought to be localized in the posterior inferior temporal gyrus (ITG), is now understood to involve a wider area of the ventral temporal cortex (VTC). Using a comprehensive set of functional MRI data and a statistically rigorous method, we determined the degree of functional animacy segregation across the VTC using a water-filling approach. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that categorization-related areas for living things and inanimate objects are distinctly separated across a wider area of the human VTC. Furthermore, the location of this functional animacy organization correlates with the degree of cortical thickness in the surrounding region.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, given the conductor. Additionally, it demonstrates the same outcome for families of Hecke-Maass newforms with varying weights in an family of elliptic modular newforms. Furthermore, the research extends a previous estimate on the distribution of Hecke L-series zeros near s=1, improving the bound from loglog T to (log T)^{o(1)} within specific ranges of T, and significantly, it proves the nonexistence of exceptional zeros for families of elliptic modular Hecke L-series, in contrast to the current reliance on numerical checks for GL_2 newforms as part of the original proof.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently influenced by a single high-transmission event, often referred to as a super-spreader event.  Statistical analysis was conducted in this study using data from the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic in Italy to assess the prevalence of these high-transmission events and assess their impact on the overall spread of the virus.  Results  revealed that R0 values associated with high transmission days were significantly higher than those on typical days, as well as days with low transmission levels.  Furthermore, modeling indicated that incorporating R0 values linked to high transmission days in a population could accelerate the spread of a virus exponentially.  This research emphasizes the critical role that high transmission events play in the dynamics of epidemics.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma \subset L(X).

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, which are crucial for understanding the Sun's activity and the behavior of the solar system. Although the Sun is frequently observed using remote sensing techniques, the data is subject to measurement errors and potential biases due to the difficulty of accurately capturing the magnetic field. The author employs a method called Stochastic Inversion of Polarimetric data (SIPol) to compare different measurement techniques and found that each approach is prone to a systematic bias in the magnetic field distribution. This bias is found to be correlated with the total magnetic field strength and varies depending on the polarimetric data used, which poses a problem for interpreting solar features and their impact on the solar system. The paper suggests that a method called Inversion by Genetic Inversion (IGenSol) can serve as a reliable reference for detecting and mitigating bias in vector magnetic field measurements, which is crucial for ensuring the accuracy of data used to interpret the Sun's activity and the solar system's behavior.

A comprehensive investigation of 600066 young star clusters from six neighboring galaxies has been carried out, involving the Andromeda galaxy, a vast expanse of the Milky Way, M87, four distinct galaxy groups, and an extensive collection of spiral and elliptical galaxies. The locations and sizes of these clusters were obtained from diverse sources, and the data were meticulously cleaned to remove the effects of star formation within the galaxies themselves. The results show that the radii of these clusters vary significantly, spanning several magnitudes, with notable influences from the host galaxies and their surroundings. The study found that the typical distances of these clusters from the galaxy centers are affected by both local galaxy density and cosmic environment density. The positions of these clusters also seem to be influenced by their surrounding environments, with clusters in high-density areas more likely to be found near the galaxy centers, while those in low-density areas often reside at the outer edges of the galaxies. The study further found that this is indicative of runaways stars escaping their orbits due to interactions with other stars, and that this is more common in galaxy mergers than in major galaxy encounters. The study also found that clusters in elliptical galaxies are typically located in more distant orbits than those in spiral galaxies, with this being more common in large galaxies than in small ones. The study used this finding to estimate that at least half of all clusters in the local group may be destroyed due to tidal forces before they age. The study used this data

To compute the decay rate of the $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$, we employ an effective theory known as Non-Relativistic Quantum Chromodynamics (NRQCD). By constructing three distinct lattice operators that can mediate this decay process, we apply the framework of lattice effective field theory. The strategy involves first determining the mass differences associated with heavy quark bound states, specifically $\Sigma_{\bar cc}^1$ and $^3S_1$, and then estimating the lattice scale using the decay rate of the $\bar cc^3S_1$ state to a lepton pair. Ultimately, the lattice-derived results for the relevant operators and mass differences are utilized to derive the decay rate of the $\eta_c$ to a two-photon final state. The outcome of this approach yields a lattice-based estimate for the form factor at two photons, resulting in a value of $0.71(10)(11)(14)$ for the $\eta_c$ decay rate.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path, but this transformation also affects the efficiency of the simulation through a severe scaling of the sign problem's severity. Our investigation into the relationship between path deformation and the Hubbard sign problem reveals that an optimal path exists for certain instances of the sign problem to be resolved. To identify this optimal path, we introduce a novel artificial neural network, trained to accomplish this task using machine learning techniques. The results of our study demonstrate the algorithm's capability to find a significantly deformed path that reduces the statistical error to the desired level with ten times fewer sampling steps in comparison to the original real axis.

This paper explores the connection between the count of highly composite integers within a specific range and the Dickman function, and demonstrates that this count closely aligns with this function for various growth rates. In contrast, when considering slightly larger super-composite integers, the count deviates significantly from the Dickman function across almost all specific time scales.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: if σ has finite support, then topological entropy is preserved (h_X = h_Y) if and only if σ itself is a topological entropy preserver (h_X = h_Y) and complexity functions are related as p_X(n) ≤ p_Y(n) ≤ (max{σ}|_A^1,n})p_X(n). Additionally, for free group morphisms τ and subshifts X, the topological entropy and complexity functions of the reversed subshift X_R are related to those of X by the inequalities (max{τ}|_A^1,n_X)a ≤ p_X_R ≤ p_X and h_X_R = h_X (h_X_R = h_X) if and only if max{τ}|_A^1 = a (min{τ}|_A^1 = a).

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as RACET0 that employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, enabling the model to seamlessly transfer its learned abilities to new, unseen tasks.
Our experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms both superset training and selective filtering approaches under unsupervised conditions.
Moreover, our results indicate that RACET0 implicitly mitigates model overconfidence issues and implicitly addresses the difficulty of unsupervised data labeling by implicitly addressing clusters of high similarity in unsupervised features.
These findings suggest that RACET0 endows the model with improved unsupervised cross-task generalization ability and more stable, reliable performance on unfamiliar, unseen tasks.

This research introduces an accelerated version of the M-arcsinh kernel Fast Independent Component Analysis, called m-arcsinh kernel-Fast ICA (m-a-r-fica). It leverages the pre-computation and indexing advantages of the m-arcsinh kernel to enable simultaneous application of multiple kernels in the original feature space, without the need to increase the dimensionality of the data. Leveraging the unique feature of the kernel, our algorithm can efficiently handle diverse types of data, including ordinal and nominal features. In fact, it is one of the very few dimensionality reduction techniques that supports nominal data. Building upon the existing m-arcsinh kernel, our algorithm further incorporates a parallel processing capability to enable the rapid computation of the kernel matrix, resulting in significant improvements in processing time. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves comparable performance to other state-of-the-art methods that utilize multiple kernel learning, but with faster processing times.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
Existing research studies on this topic have been comprehensively examined.
Key characteristics of the gaming industry were identified and their connections to broader market dynamics discussed.
In addition, several potential areas for further research within this field were briefly highlighted.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical challenge, as the selection of hyperparameters significantly influences the balance between private learning performance and safeguarded privacy guarantees. Initially, we explore the effectiveness of a private hyperparameter tuning technique, specifically the grid search, on the evaluation metrics of the optimized model. A thorough examination of its limitations reveals that, despite its simplicity, it has several shortcomings, including an excessively large computational demand, restricted applicability to a narrow set of hyperparameters, and search patterns that may not reflect their counterparts in unencrypted learning. In light of these constraints, we introduce an enhanced optimization framework, leveraging the efficiency and flexibility of the grid search while maintaining its performance benefits, resulting in a faster and more adaptable tuning process with improved flexibility.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

The Euclid satellite's imaging instrument (NISP) will be instrumental in studying the expansion and geometry of the universe, as well as the distribution of matter on a cosmic scale, from the beginning of time to the end of the universe. A key concern for the Euclid mission is the impact of readout noise on the accuracy of the measurements, especially in the regions of the universe closest to the universe's visible light. Our analysis indicates that a new method of processing the NISP's data can effectively neutralise the impact of readout noise on the measurement of the universe's geometry and its contents across all regions of the universe's history, while maintaining the integrity of the data collected in the universe's more recent history.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to analyze data from 14400 red giant stars in the Milky Way disk, using chemical compositions to categorize them. A two-component model was fitted to the spectra of these stars to determine their unique elemental compositions, specifically iron and alpha elements. The model showed that the stars can be divided into two distinct populations based on their chemical compositions, with no overlap between the groups. Furthermore, analyzing the differences between actual and predicted spectral features revealed interesting insights into the stars' chemical properties. Specifically, the population with more complex chemical compositions was found to be closer to the galactic center, while the population with simpler chemical compositions was further away. Additionally, this study was expanded to include a larger dataset of red giants, using nearly 50000 stars from the APOGEE-2 survey, which confirmed the findings of the smaller survey.

The spread of rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic on social media posed a significant threat to public information security. To understand the underlying mechanisms of online rumor propagation, we analyzed the content of real-world rumors that circulated on Sina Weibo in China. Through content segmentation and the use of BERT for text representation, we identified key factors contributing to the spread of rumors, which included the use of keywords, emoticons, source credibility, source types, source locations, and the framing of the news. Based on these findings, we proposed a multi-dimensional linearity score (MLS) to measure the influence of user posts about COVID-19 on social media. The effectiveness of the MLS score was validated through experiments, where it outperformed existing methods in predicting the propagation of online rumors. Moreover, the MLS score enabled the identification of high-risk groups and the ranking of topics by potential for the spread of rumors.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by exploring the relationship between a galaxy and its surrounding universe. Specifically, the correlation between the size of a galaxy and its surrounding halo has emerged as a potential tool for distance estimation. Researchers have investigated this relationship further, focusing on the connection between gas halos and planetary nebulae within galaxies in the Fornax cluster. By utilizing deep near-infrared imaging of galaxies in the Fornax Deep Survey, the team was able to identify and study the planetary nebulae within these galaxies. Through analysis of the nebulae's distribution, researchers were able to estimate the distances to the galaxies in question. This method has been applied to a sample of early-type galaxies in the southern portion of the Fornax cluster, and the resulting distance measurements were compared to established estimates. The findings suggest that this technique may offer a precise and reliable means of determining the distance to galaxies, and could prove useful for future studies of the universe. Additionally, researchers have discovered that a galaxy's size appears to be related to its distance from the galaxy cluster, and this relationship has been formally defined.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from patients undergoing continuous monitoring. This monitoring system is an invaluable resource for medical professionals, enabling them to diagnose and treat patients more effectively. However, manually processing and analyzing this data manually is both laborious and time-consuming. Although some researchers have attempted to automate this process by developing intelligent frameworks to assist medical staff, these tools often struggle to balance performance with usability due to the labor-intensive nature of processing large data sets. To address this challenge, we introduce LifeStream, a high-performance stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data sets collected on a regular basis. LifeStream is built upon Apache Flink and is capable of processing multiple data sets simultaneously, allowing for real-time analysis and diagnosis. Furthermore, LifeStream is user-friendly and easy to use, allowing medical professionals to focus on their patients rather than their code. As a result, our engine is also open-source and available to the research community for further development and collaboration.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is considered a key decision with far-reaching implications on the model's performance. The success of various loss functions, such as cross-entropy and activation functions like softmax and Sigmoid, is well-established in the context of classification tasks. However, there's a lack of comprehensive knowledge about their underlying patterns of impact. This paper aims to contribute to this knowledge by gathering and analyzing a diverse set of trained neural network models on multiple datasets, which enables us to isolate loss function changes from other factors like network architecture and training procedure. Through this isolated investigation, we've identified consistent performance rankings of loss functions across different models and only a few instances where the order varies when applied to different datasets. This research provides a solid foundation for the design of novel loss functions by revealing the underlying principles of their impact.
A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition strategy and a cohesive zone model to crystalline nucleation, coupled with a percolation criterion to track the crystalline network formation. Consequently, the model simulates strain-induced crystallization's nucleation, growth, and resulting mechanical and thermal properties changes. Initially, the governing equations were solved using quasi-static assumptions, and the results indicated that applying a gradual, strain-induced crystallization model yields more realistic outcomes than abrupt models. Subsequently, the focus expanded to analyzing the mechanical and thermal properties of the material within the crystalline phase, including its melting point. Ultimately, a fully coupled model was developed to explore strain-induced crystallization's complete evolution, including nucleation, properties development, and melting points within the crystals phase.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we used a neel-type superconducting gap and a spin-triplet p-wave Fermi surface pairing potential with spin-orbit coupling. Our calculations demonstrated that nematic superconductivity can emerge from the weak-coupling stage under specific doping conditions and is very sensitive to the relative strength of the mass term and spin-orbit coupling. Notably, our model predicts a unique phenomenon where Neel-type triplet pairs exhibit Pauli paramagnetism, in contrast to conventional s-wave and other triplet pairs that are magnetically saturated. The response of the superconductor to the magnetic field is dictated by the interplay between the mass term, spin-orbit coupling, and the superconducting gap, and this can be used as a distinguishing feature in experimental measurements of the superconductor's magnetic susceptibility.

One of the most significant hurdles in robotics is the need for precise guidance during learning tasks, such as robotics. In this study, a novel meta-algorithm is presented that enables a robot to learn from preliminary feedback provided by a human instructor. This type of feedback helps to refine the role of the guiding data, allowing the robot to learn more efficiently. The proposed algorithm is designed to incorporate this feedback automatically, without the need for explicit segmentation of the corrective feedback. Additionally, experiments are conducted on the robot's ability to learn new and related tasks from both the combined dataset of initial and corrective feedback, as well as from the initial feedback alone.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure involves a memory of one symbol, which results in efficient hardware implementation and minimal delay optimization. However, this simple memory system leads to suboptimal symbol timing. By introducing an improved model that considers additional delay parameters, a more precise ideal differential detection method can be developed. Consequently, the new scheme is able to achieve efficient delay processing, allowing even Conventional Differential Resolved CPM (DCRCPM) to benefit from it. Conventional differential detection methods are widely applied due to their effectiveness and simplicity, and by formulating their detection as maximum a posteriori estimation, the problem of timing optimization becomes more manageable. Using the CDRCPM signal as an example, the paper shows that the optimal cost function derived is consistent with the purpose of detection, and the algorithm is also demonstrated to be beneficial for other types of CPM signals.

New findings from 1D core-collapse simulations of various massive stars have been found in conflict with the previously established connection between black-hole neutron-star mergers and the phenomenon of tidal disruption. According to tidal-disruption events, there should be some neutron stars merging with black-holes while still being illuminated by the neutron-star's light as it is torn apart. Contrary to this expectation, recent data from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration showed no evidence of such mergements. This discrepancy has been addressed by re-evaluating the fundamental aspects of the collapse of the stellar core, rather than modifications to the equation of state of nuclear matter. Based on core-collapse simulations that cover a broad range of stellar mass and spin, along with the resulting population-synthesis calculations, there should actually be more black-hole neutron-star mergers detected by multi-messenger astronomy than the current data indicates, a conclusion supported primarily by the predicted rate of these mergers from supernovae events. Furthermore, the proposed detector sensitivity improvements in the next few years should help resolve the tidal-disruption event merger upper limit estimate and potentially detect actual cases of such mergers, although it should also detect more black-hole neutron-star merger events than currently expected.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio between the spacetime's vacuum compressibility and equilibrium compressibility, which is approximately $10^{-66}$ times Planck units. The present study aims to examine the compressibility of spacetime in the context of thermal radiation, with a particular focus on thermal fields that are confined within a cavity. The results show a significant deviation from the original finding, with the ratio exhibiting a unique pattern of variation as the temperature changes, leading to the ultra-high values observed in the extreme低温 range and the extreme高温 range.

Current deep learning techniques for removing rain from images have achieved impressive results in simulated environments, but their performance deteriorates significantly in real-world scenarios due to the unrealistic artificial rain generated for training. The high dimensionality of potential rain patterns contributes to this issue. This paper presents an innovative approach that simultaneously learns to generate and synthesize rain-free images through a novel multi-task framework. We designed a two-way discrete translation learning framework, enabling the model to both remove pre-existing rain and generate rain on clear images in a single unified network. The introduction of sparsity constraints and shared latent space ensures efficient classification of rain patterns and enhances the model's ability to synthesize diverse rain patterns. The resulting model demonstrates outstanding performance in simultaneously generating and removing rain, with the ability to generate highly realistic rain patterns validated through extensive quantitative analysis and visual comparisons.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature of the language, influenced by specific theoretical assumptions. This issue is exemplified by the model companions of first-order theories in the same language, with notable differences in outcomes. In contrast, taking into account model companions in the same theory but an expanded language presents an intriguing scenario. Specifically, the relationship between first-order and second-order arithmetic is influenced by the existence of a solution to the Continuum problem. The existence or non-existence of a solution can be determined by examining the model companion of first-order arithmetic with the axioms of a certain class of set-theoretic statements in the same language. The outcomes of this analysis mirror those of computing the model companion of a first-order theory in a more complex language. In effect, the complexity increases from classifying models up to a certain equivalence level to another level, with the difference being modelable within the original language but not across the higher level.

This study establishes conditions for positive solutions to exist on a bounded area in n-dimensional space for a problem involving the Q-curvature of conformal geometry and a related higher-order curvature, denoted as I4, specifically when certain conditions are met for a given function f, including when it has a positive average value multiplied by a specific integral over the bounded area. Additionally, a no solution case is proved under different integral conditions that are comparable to those found in related studies. Furthermore, a large parameter case is discussed, and an explicit formula for a positive solution is derived for a specific scenario where the bounded area is a ball and the given function f meets certain conditions, leading to an exact solution when the parameter lambda is sufficiently large.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial for creating effective prevention strategies. This study aims to develop a set of criteria to assess drug consumption risk, focusing on personality traits as key elements. We used the Five Factor Model of personality to create a set of criteria that can evaluate an individual's risk of drug consumption. Data from 1,155 university students was employed to both design and validate the set of criteria. Data analysis revealed that the set of criteria is consistent and can be broken down into two main dimensions: a set of indicators associated with the Five Factor Model of personality (accounting for 31.2% of the variance) and a set of indicators not part of the Five Factor Model (accounting for 11.5% of the variance). Additionally, we compared different versions of the set of criteria to optimize its functionality.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning pairs that focus on if-then relationships.  The complete ATOMIC dataset comprises nearly 37,000 text descriptions, but a carefully selected subset of about 4,300 statements excludes tautological statements and demonstrates a strong performance of over 60% accuracy when evaluated through a sophisticated baseline model.

Portfolio optimization is a complex task in finance, and solving it using the HHL algorithm for linear systems presents new challenges. This study develops an adaptation of the HHL algorithm, NISQ-HHL, and applies it to solve the Hessian system of equations. By modifying the algorithm, it becomes possible to retrieve the solution directly in the form of a vector. Furthermore, by integrating the NISQ-HHL and a post-processing method, a solution is obtained that is both feasible and optimal. Two hardware tests were conducted using IBM's quantum computers, and the solution was also solved using classical computers. Finally, by comparing the results, it is shown that NISQ-HHL with post-processing is a suitable approach for portfolio optimization.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampled features between the two encoders, effectively reducing the sampling rate discrepancy. This approach is integrated with the FET-ASR speech recognition framework, and when combined with the multi-modal learning loss, it allows for the exchange of learned representations from both encodes. This method is particularly useful given the prevalence of unpaired text datasets in modern datasets. Our proposed solution is trained on the FET-ASR framework and a subset of the Librispeech dataset, and the results indicate a significant performance boost of 2.5 dB in Word Error Rate when compared to the baseline, ASR-only training.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved unless cross-sections pass through the centroid of the shape. Therefore, a specific value is proposed, representing the optimal average cross-section through non-centroidal points, and its application is demonstrated on various polyhedra and polytopes.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. Specifically, it studies the asymptotic properties of its initial $k$ positions, represented as $\pi_n(1,\dots,k)$. Given that parking functions can be considered as independent and identically distributed random variables, the theorem states that the uniform parking distribution converges to its expected value based on its probability mass function. Furthermore, the rate of convergence is found to be $O(n^{-1})$, which is the same for both the total variation distance and the Kullback-Leibler distance. Notably, this result implies that the first $k$ positions of the first non-cyclic permutation converge with a rate of $O(n^{-1/2})$, in contrast to the original parking scenario.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires are zero-resistance in the presence of a strong magnetic field, which leads to a question about the nature of the measurement setup. Using narrow gating of nanowires, we observe a transition from insulating to superconducting states in a phase diagram. The critical field boundary exhibits linear growth with a critical exponent of one. The exponent is consistent with quantum phase slip model predictions and contradicts the Coulomb blockade model.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, but a complete understanding of its physical and chemical properties remained elusive due to conflicting atmospheric models yielding broad atmospheric temperature estimates. This research aimed to address this issue by utilizing the newly developed machine learning-based spectral analysis tool, APOLLO, to create a precise atmospheric temperature of 555+/-10 K for GJ 229B, as well as accurate surface gravity and chemical abundance estimates. The newly acquired atmospheric parameters were supported by multiple lines of evidence, leading to the development of specialized low-temperature theoretical models that matched the observed spectrum of GJ 229B across a wide wavelength range. Furthermore, the temperature of 555 K was corroborated by the behavior of water in the atmosphere of GJ 229B, as simulated with 3D radiative-convective general purpose codes.

Our study offers an exploration of the lattice QCD calculations for deep inelastic scattering, focusing on interactions with a quark-gluon plasma. In this research, we differentiate between scalar and vector correlations, and the distinction between vector scalar correlations is linked to pion form factors through the use of dispersion relations. In addition, the mass of the proton can be determined from scalar correlations using chiral perturbation theory. By analyzing scalar correlations through a machine learning approach, specifically using quark eigenvalues, we can make preliminary comparisons with experimental data.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research, we no longer assume that the camera's intrinsics remain constant, instead allowing for varying fields of view and lens characteristics. Our prediction process involves converting the video from each camera's perspective to a 3D model, specifically a shape representation known as a Dual Atlas, which encapsulates both the object's appearance and spatial arrangement. We then generate sequences of novel images from additional camera angles by rendering the 3D model from those perspectives. Our approach excels in handling complex objects with multiple components, occlusions, and objects that change shape, as demonstrated in our experiments.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. By analyzing the coupled system's propagation, two types of outputs were identified, corresponding to energy transfer between the two orthogonal modes. The use of inter-orbital coupling may lead to the development of stable multi-channel communication systems and the design of novel devices that manipulate light based on orbital characteristics.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay of multiple factors including ventilation, air recirculation, aerosol generation and deposition, as well as人员活动. In this study, a computational approach utilizing well-mixed models was examined to predict the spread of diseases, specifically through example calculations involving SARS-CoV-2 on a bus in Boston during late November 2020. Although it was demonstrated that well-mixed models could accurately estimate viral exposure under certain conditions, significant discrepancies were found between its predictions and a more detailed computational fluid dynamics simulation. While it was observed that well-mixed models were sensitive to ventilation rates and person-to-person spacing, they were less affected by the rate of airflow that recirculates and surface deposition of the virus. Given these findings, caution is advised against using simplified models with high viral exposure potential without first comparing them to more realistic simulations.

Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the birefringent scattering of x-rays when interacting with two combined optical lasers, considering various possible outcomes. To aid in detecting quantum vacuum effects experimentally, our analysis focuses particularly on situations where x-ray photons show differences not just in polarization, but also in direction of propagation and potential energy changes.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. This property is applicable to both classical and quantum settings. In this study, we've completely characterized classical unclonable encryption schemes, showing that they're essentially a more complex form of one-time pads. We've also completely characterized one-time clonable classical schemes, showing that even a small amount of extra information beyond a secure one-time pad enables the ability to create an exact copy of a given ciphertext. These characterizations are supported by completing the work started in the paperarXiv:1905.00134 for several open problems.

This study confirms that physical layer authentication in mobile communications
can be effectively achieved in additive white Gaussian noise environments,
despite the absence of secret keys. We analyze the security of this type of
authentication method and provide an estimation of the failure rates for both
impersonation and substitution attacks. Our research also offers design
strategies to minimize these attack success probabilities. Furthermore, our
findings suggest that even a limited number of captured transmissions can be
enough to enable successful attacks. However, this number can be accurately
estimated given the number of observations available.

We utilized the full tight-binding model to investigate the flat bands within the twisted metal dichalcogenides, specifically those based on MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$. On an $\sqrt{3}\times \sqrt{3}$ moiré lattice, we identified an additional small pocket at the K point that possesses flat bands with energy ranges overlapping the van Hove singularities. By applying the random phase approximation, we discovered that plasmons residing on this small pocket exhibit a plasma frequency that is significantly higher than that on the large pocket. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent width of the plasma peak can be effectively described by the scattering rate derived from the time-dependent approach, in contrast to the conventional parabolic bands where this rate shows insufficient agreement. Notably, the position of the plasma peak shifts due to Coulomb interaction and moves towards higher energy levels as temperature decreases. The features observed in calculations align with experimental results from interband scattering loss measurements on fs-TMPES. The proposed system provides a feasible platform for investigating strongly correlated physics, specifically the scattering rate linearly related to momentum and temperature.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a connection with $\rho$ and demonstrate that if the soliton is geometric steady, the potential function is constant. Additionally, if the soliton is geometric expanding and the manifold's Ricci curvature is non-negative, the soliton must be $\eta$-Ricci soliton with $\lambda = 1/2$. Finally, we derive a lower bound for the function $f$ in terms of $\lambda, p,$ and $\rho$.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
star winds. However, in some cases, planetary magnetospheres are also affected by
the external magnetic field of their host star.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SOPE) enables the generation of strong spin-orientation at a ferromagnetic interface due to high spin-orbit materials. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems involving interfaces between heavy metals and superconductors or topological insulators and ferromagnets. In the case of interface between 3d transition metal Cobalt and Bi with its large spin-orbit coupling, there has not been a comprehensive experimental investigation. In this work, time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr effect and linear optical transmission measurements were performed to study the Bi/Co multilayer and the influence of interface scattering on the SOPE. It was found that spin-orientation at the Bi surface develops in close analogy to the SOPE found in other ferromagnetic interfaces. Interestingly, spin-orientation at the Bi surface is not simply the sum of spin-orientation at the Co/Co interfaces. Experimental data indicated that spin-orientation is significantly affected by the degree of scattering at the Bi/Co interface. In fact, Bi/Co interfaces with higher interface scattering led to increased spin-orientation.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha}+B/r^{\alpha}+C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained for various values of $\alpha$, demonstrating that they correspond to solutions in spaces between Euclidean and fractal spacetimes. Successful comparison with existing literature and numerical results confirms the method's reliability and accuracy.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it appears in recent works, relates to regularisation. This study proves that k-Lipschitz neural networks exhibit a reduced sensitivity to variations in input data, thereby demonstrating their effectiveness in generalisation. It is further shown that such networks possess an upper bound on the expected generalisation error that grows with the square of the network's parameter count. We also provide a theoretical upper limit on k-Lipschitz network capacity, proving their similarity to networks with constrained weights. Given these benefits, we propose a regularisation term based on the network's Lipschitz constant and evaluate its generalisation effects. It is found that this approach yields enhanced performance compared to networks with constrained weights, particularly in scenarios of over-parametrisation.

Sequential neural network models have achieved significant success in
addressing the Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging task across numerous languages.
These architectures take advantage of the sequential nature of text data,
which conventional non-sequential models like Conditional Random Fields (CRF)
do not fully consider. In this study, we investigate the capability of
sequential models to capture the agreement phenomena in Basque, a language
that exhibits complex morphological structures. We compare the performance of
a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model against strong non-sequential baselines,
including a Bi-directional Fast Text model and a CRF model enhanced with an
LSTM component. Our results demonstrate that the LSTM model outperforms the
other models, achieving a substantial improvement of 2.15 F-scores over the
best Basque-specific non-sequential model. Notably, the gain achieved by the
LSTM model is 5 F-scores more than a standard Bi-LSTM model, highlighting the
benefit of incorporating an LSTMLayer to the CRF model.

HD80606b is a planet with a highly eccentric orbit around its star, which significantly varies in temperature. This extreme fluctuation in the planet's atmosphere enables a unique opportunity to study atmospheric composition through spectroscopy. Due to its scientific importance, the planet will be observed multiple times with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). However, some of its spectral data appears to be influenced by the movement of the planet in its orbit. This study conducts precise analysis using ground-based telescopes to account for the planet's movement and enhances its orbital data, which can aid in planning efficient observations with the JWST.

Customized digital games effectively motivate patients during physical therapy sessions,
but creating the perfect program that balances learning about the activity and exercising
is a complex challenge. Existing methods of evaluating scaffold levels only assess
cognitive understanding, neglecting to consider the physiological aspects. This research
introduces a two-phase approach to designing activity programs, incorporating physical
exercises and cognitive scaffolds for better execution. It also suggests employing
simulation models to test both levels of scaffolds simultaneously. As an example, this
approach is applied to a table tennis rehabilitation program, utilizing simulation models
to test the programs' effectiveness.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan lepton pair production in the Standard Model and introduce vector leptoquarks as new particles that could mediate this process. Calculating corrections to a specific particle's impact using QCD, we determine the most significant corrections at the NLO level, utilizing both analytical and numerical methods. These calculations are incorporated into a widely-used QCD simulation tool, allowing us to study the leptoquark's effects on the standard lepton invariant spectrum.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups such as pregnant women, children, and patients undergoing frequent follow-up imaging. Using complementary computed tomography (CT) images to create synthetic PET images based on the biological and physical principles underlying PET scanning can enable a safer PET scan with fewer PET detections and more accurate and reliable results. This paper introduces a new, integrated multimodal machine learning framework that lever next-generation neural networks to develop a direct mapping from low-dose PET and CT images to more accurate PET images, thereby improving the quality of images obtained from less effective PET scans.

The issue of tailoring news content to individual users while respecting their data has long plagued online platforms. Although the personalization of web content has reached new heights in the last decade, these advancements have largely overlooked small- to medium-sized enterprises and news organizations specifically. Many online publications still rely on rudimentary personalization techniques, primarily driven by profiling methods that infringe on user privacy. This personalization/privacy gap can be bridged by exploring and integrating alternative, user-centric personalization approaches in web applications. This paper undertakes a in-depth investigation into web personalization/privacy challenges, potential solutions, and relevant technical developments, ultimately aiming to suggest more equitable personalization/privacy models for both users and businesses.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations develops from the structure of individual sentences. This paper explores the connection between CT and the development of machine systems that identify relationships between sentence mentions in the same language. By comparing the structural patterns of coreferential mentions in a specific machine learning dataset, we investigate whether current machine systems that recognize connections between mentions, called co-reference solvers, are effectively utilizing the structural patterns that influence how mentions are related. Our research reveals that while nearer mentions are generally more likely to be related, this tendency is significantly enhanced by trained machine systems, particularly when considering specific contextual factors. This evidence shows that CT provides a useful framework for understanding the development of co-reference recognition systems.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

The rising intricacy of modern adaptable systems demands elevated automation in their configuration process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated workflow integration. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved human understanding via metric-driven optimization. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to configuring a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable a detailed exploration that reveals the interplay between the operator growth rate and the complexity-parity oscillation pattern inherent in some systems.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals within indoor spaces. Researchers have tested various techniques to calculate distances between devices based on signal measurements, turning to machine learning as a means of comparison. This study introduces three machine learning methods to estimate distances between a WiFi router and a receiving device, with the aim of identifying the most effective method. As the primary indicator, this research collects Received Signal Strength values and uses them to calculate distances in steps of 0.5 meters over a 10-meter indoor range. Notably, data was gathered in 0.5-meter increments to allow for more accurate testing and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that the most successful approach to signal processing is utilizing raw Received Signal Strength values, with the best method being Support Vector Regression, achieving a standard deviation of only 0.25 meters.

For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson sphere as a primary target. A Dyson sphere is an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for civilization level 2 on the Kardashev scale. However, constructing such a structure around a stellar black hole poses significant challenges. This study demonstrates that, in theory, a Dyson sphere could still function if constructed to orbit a stellar black hole, albeit with important design considerations. A Dyson sphere would need multiple layers of solar collectors at varying distances to avoid being sucked into the star, which in turn affects its stability and observable characteristics. Using a solar black hole as a model, it is estimated that an optimal single-layer Dyson sphere would spin at an incredibly high frequency, emitting a distinctive infrared signal. If a Dyson sphere exists around a black hole, it may be detectable through its unique orbital periods and resonance frequencies.

Network-based services are crucial for society's functioning, and as they become more relied upon, ensuring they meet agreed-upon quality standards is becoming increasingly vital. A key aspect of this is detecting and addressing any agreements breaches in a timely and effective manner. A novel approach to this issue involves a decentralized system where users monitor service performance and report any discrepancies. This system, however, is susceptible to inaccuracies due to user misreporting. A more sophisticated method employs a network of mutual watchdogs to verify reports and pinpoint areas experiencing issues. This approach, tested through simulations, was found to be capable of accurately identifying discrepancies in a timely manner while avoiding false alarms.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge for energy recovery linacs, hindering their performance. To tackle this issue, various strategies are being explored, including modifying the electron beam's transverse profile and changing the bunch profile. So far, most studies into beam breakup have been conducted using idealized models that don't account for real cavity characteristics and field calculations based on boundary element methods. In this research, a more practical approach is taken by incorporating actual measured cavities and using time-domain particle tracking to evaluate the impact of different beam filling patterns on beam breakup. The results from this study reveal that specific internal cavity fields play a crucial role in determining growth rates and can even switch from negative to positive, thus influencing the severity of the beam breakup instability.

To determine the neutron flux in a 3D scintillator detector designed for time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) fluorescence measurements, traditional methods involve attaching an activated standard sample to it.
