The research delves into analyzing the relationship between the scrollar invariants of plane curves and the successive minima of orders in number fields, and establishes the inequality $\mu \leq |\Delta|^{1/2}\lambda_1\dots \lambda_n < 2\mu$, where $\mu$ is related to the log-canonical threshold of a general curve in a specific family parametrized by its Weierstrass coefficients. The research also establishes the bound $|\Delta|^{1/2}\lambda_1\dots \lambda_n < 2\mu$ for any number field

We present an innovative 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy technique using two probes, enabling dual gas pairs to be measured in one experiment. In a novel application, this method allows for the simultaneous measurement of pressure, temperature, and oxygen-nitrogen ratios in a single shot. By leveraging machine learning models, we successfully mapped the complex features of the overlapping fs/ps spectra and interpreted the information they contain. Nitrogen and oxygen have distinct spectral features in the near-infrared, enabling precise pressure and temperature measurements for N2 gas, and an O2/N2 ratio in a single gas mixture. We utilized an fs laser to record the rotational spectrum of O2 and a ps laser for N2, while a high-speed fs laser system recorded multiple spectra in a very short time. This technique represents a significant advancement in the capability of fs/ps CARS to measure multiple gas pairs simultaneously.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations in explaining how small particles overcome friction and quickly form planets. A more recent concept proposes the existence of a turbulent, ring-like structure in the middle of some protoplanetary disks that generates the heat and conditions necessary for planet formation. This study uses observations and simulations to characterize this torus feature and explore its role in planet formation. By analyzing a large set of photos of disks, it demonstrates that the torus is actually stable and produces the right conditions for particles to clump together and form the building blocks of planets. Furthermore, it suggests that the turbulent motion within the torus could be a key factor in core accretion.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting edge modes that transport information.  Here, we investigate an setup with two disconnected regions in a quantum Hall system, and an upstream current in region A.  The correlated electron fluctuations are captured by a boundary CFT, allowing us to compute the dc current in region B induced by electron interactions.  Our findings show that neutral operators at the edge can cause an upstream current to produce a downstream current.  Notably, this effect persists in the weak coupling limit but vanishes for both boson and fermion operators.  The outcome is governed by the type and charge neutrality of the represented operators.  This effect may have implications for the active control of electron flow in quantum Hall circuits using edge mode operators.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action, demonstrating that quantum multiplication by a basis element preserves the basis \bar{Θ}'s structure, with coefficients expressible as non-negative polynomials in q^(1/2) and q^(-1/2).

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a resilient and robust
distributed learning system that operates without the need for a central server.
We specifically focus on minimizing the risk of data being manipulated by a
malicious participant who has the ability to disrupt the learning process. To
achieve this goal, we propose an innovative distributionally robust
algorithm named DR-DSGD, which utilizes the split method and incorporates a
distributionally robust optimization technique. By using the normal
distribution to model the noise and applying a Witten-Hastie estimator to
handle the skewed data produced by the optimization, DR-DSGD is capable of
effectively learning the data in a way that mirrors the behavior of the ideal
gradient descent method. We also provide theoretical support for this
approach and demonstrate through experiments that it outperforms existing
distributed learning techniques in the presence of a malicious participant.

We have examined past methods of computing the hard-disk model, a classic system in statistical mechanics, whose behavior varies based on how much space the disks occupy. Many studies on this model have preceded the availability of fast computers, thus paving the way for the field of computer simulations in physics. We discuss past methods of simulating the hard-disk model and discuss their benefits and limitations, as well as the development of new algorithms that can provide reliable data even in densely packed scenarios.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment fraud, exploit new technology through poorly secured cryptocurrency contracts, with the recent Forsage case in question. Forsage developers created a pyramid scheme that relied on the Ethereum blockchain for user data security, with nearly $40 million invested by approximately 30,000 individuals by early May 2021. An analysis of the contract's code, which contained a vulnerability allowing Forsage admins to steal funds, combined with an examination of transaction records, as well as the info provided by the developers on their website and social media platforms, revealed the true extent of the operation's damage.

The number of globular clusters in the Milky Way is still incomplete identified. In this study, the VVV survey was utilized to investigate 19 globular cluster candidates discovered within the southern galactic bulge region. We obtained color-magnitude diagrams and measured the point source properties in each candidate. We found that 15 of the candidates were actually foreground sources, leaving only 4 confirmed as genuine globular clusters. The mass function of these clusters will be the subject of further investigation in a subsequent article.

A precise understanding of differential cross-section differences between the Drell-Yan and proton-proton processes in high colliding energy environments is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of proton structure in quantum chromodynamics. To achieve this, inclusive measurements are combined with sensitive, process-specific contributions, known as soft functions, that capture interactions between isolated final-state objects and low-energy gluons. In this study, we examine the impact of massively quarks on such prescriptions up to a certain order of precision, both in the Drell-Yan and proton-proton processes. A theoretical inconsistency arises in certain kinematic regions when using these prescriptions for isolated massive quarks. To resolve this, we derive exclusive hadronic matrix elements for these processes in a quark-mass regulated scheme. These new elements effectively incorporate the necessary corrections to ensure a precise, physically accurate description of isolated massive quark effects in a certain direct mass range.

We examine the calculation of electron optical properties within a wide range of temporal frequencies using a detailed method that accounts for how light interacts with matter in a way that respects fundamental symmetry principles. This approach is based on the principles of quantum mechanics and the mathematical model used to describe the system. It involves considering the entire set of possible states that the electrons can be in, both when they are being affected by light and when they are not. It allows for very precise calculations of optical properties for materials of various types, including those made of atoms held together by chemical bonds, two-dimensional surfaces and models with periodic patterns. It even allows researchers to examine the movement of electrons within the material as it is being affected by light, which can be done in real-time.

In this context, we analyze a specific class of holographic tensor networks, known as invariant multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz (iMERA) states, which serve as approximate representations of systems with linear growth and power-law decay. These states exhibit a form of holo-nonrenormalizability, which enables a novel decoding scheme that generalizes previous methods. This scheme is robust against perturbations and highly efficient, requiring only polynomial resources. As an outcome, these renormalizable network states exhibit a numerical Heisenberg time scale for thermalization in the bulk, thermalization of boundary theories experiences Heisenberg time in a logarithmic scale, and these network states exhibit both logarithmic and Heisenberg time scales for thermalization. These features align with expectations from the holographic principle under the dual AdS/CFT correspondence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these states exhibit strong code-like characteristics, which allows them to correct a broad range of erasures in a nonlocal manner, generalizing the concept of perfect codes.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilizes a dual-mode classical stochastic framework.  Based on this model, researchers examined how a thermal bath's frequency and strength affect the chromophore's recovery of energy from light.  Surprisingly, minor changes in either parameter resulted in significant recovery variations, even when the chromophore's energy states were balanced.  This sensitive dependence on external conditions has no precedent in traditional retinal chemistry theories and suggests that retinal chromophores might be highly susceptible to environmental fluctuations within proteins.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results but their
performance advantages aren't always evident for well-behaved processes. This
study undertakes a thorough examination of process variants prediction using
multiple approaches, including traditional methods and advanced deep-learning
models such as CRP2. Our findings indicate that for processes with a moderate
degree of variability, traditional methods can be as effective as deep-learning
models, delivering better results with greater efficiency.

The primary goal of this research is to employ graph theory and network analysis techniques to examine online discussions surrounding social issues by parsing Twitter posts. Specifically, we focus on users who actively engaged in conversations about the Izmir earthquake following its occurrence on October 30, 2020. By applying clustering algorithms to the resulting user network, we can identify key participants who actively promoted certain ideas or behaviors. Clustering results show that more than half of the active users were isolated, but three major clusters were also identified. One cluster consisted of users who shared positive messages and advocated for helping those affected, while another cluster was comprised of conspiracy theorists who promoted misinformation about alleged government manipulation of the earthquake for political gain. The remaining cluster was made up of users who disseminated false information about the location of the earthquake's epicenter, which had significant implications for rescue operations. Our findings can be utilized to better understand the spread of both beneficial and harmful information on Twitter and guide the development of more effective strategies for promoting accurate information during natural disasters.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text also presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and the relationship between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces is explored. Additionally, implications for Toeplitz operators are discussed.

Researchers analyzed 14 ultraviolet wavelength spectra from the 1985 AD Leo solar flare, focusing on continuum radiation between 290-365 nanometers. They discovered that existing theoretical models of stellar atmospheres failed to explain the observed spectral features. A combination of observed H-alpha and UV data best matched the near-UV spectrum, indicating extremely high temperatures of 30-40 million Kelvin during the peak of the flare.

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models and numerical simulations to examine how the system evolves over time. Analyzing a two-period PT-symmetric network made of alternating PT-symmetric unit cells, this study derives key insights from time-dependent simulations that align with existing research. Notably, this simulation allows for a more accurate observation of the transition between PT-symmetric and broken phases. Furthermore, this study reveals conditions under which the PT-symmetric phase enables the coherent perfect absorption-lasing effect, something that cannot always be predicted from broken phase parameters. Lastly, this research confirms that a specific input intensity threshold exists to trigger the coherent perfect absorption-lasing phenomenon.

Researchers have studied the dynamics of Boolean networks (BNs) that feature multi-node interactions and self-interactions, particularly those involving pairs of nodes. Such networks are commonly used models for describing systems with widespread connections, as they balance realistic representations with manageable complexity. We developed an extended version of the BN framework to accommodate higher-order interactions and then investigated their dynamics through analytical methods, numerical simulations, and a BN state capacity approach. Our results reveal that higher-order interactions significantly impact the networks' behavior, leading to distinct dynamic phases and a crucial relationship between interaction order and system size. These insights pave the way for exploring higher-order interactions in BNs, PNs, and neural networks that utilize these interactions.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in diverse applications such as perception, planning, and operation of robots. Nonetheless, these models often struggle with inconsistencies and inaccuracies due to the varied point sampling techniques employed in different scanners and devices. Neural network point cloud smoothers have shown promise in rectifying such issues. However, applying them requires either prior knowledge of how points were sampled or fine-tuning for each new point cloud technology. In response, we propose a flexible framework called TPC that allows for the seamless integration of smoothing networks with different point cloud technologies by performing virtual cross-sampling of the input points. This enables enhanced point cloud processing and robot operation, demonstrated through a teleoperation system that achieves smooth and consistent virtual wall navigation with the TPC framework, but struggles when it's removed, leading to erratic and inaccurate wall following.

We investigate medium access control methods for Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, specifically analyzing the impact of their channel access mechanisms on radar system design, data processing, and performance. In our observations, we classify modern MAC protocols into two categories - time-based and counting-based, and assess Slotted ALOHA and Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) by examining their MAC overhead, resource utilization, and scalability. In our testing, we observe that ALOHA's simplicity provides A_k MAC depth, but its scalability is limited to low FMCW radar network sizes. Conversely, CSMA's two-hop connectivity results in $(k-1)$ MAC depth, but excessive contention periods arise in larger radar networks when access attempts are made during the $(k-1)^{th}$ MAC slot. These issues highlight the need to re-evaluate and potentially enhance existing FMCW radar MAC protocols to accommodate multi-hop wireless radar network applications.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
Specifically, we employ shared and time-specific factors to simultaneously
minimize a loss function that balances graph and time sequence attention.
To address scenarios where time sequence data is scarce or non-existent for
certain time steps, we incorporate a time embedding matrix to enhance
time triplet representation learning. Our unified framework is particularly
effective in scenarios with unbalanced time sequences. Moreover, we propose
a flexible framework that is device-agnostic and capable of employing multi-scale
factorizations. Our experiments demonstrate that Time-LowFER is a state-of-the-art
model that outperforms prominent time embedding and time-enhanced factorization
baselines across multiple datasets.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to identify complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this technique, the RPA polar diagram's complexity of zero confirms the validity of an RPA eigenenergy. The complex RPA polar diagram complexity can be expressed as the sum of RPA log-residues and odd integrands integrals. A case study on the $^{16}$O oxygen-16 nucleus demonstrates that the complex RPA log-residues and odd integrands integrals both contribute to the RPA polar diagram complexity, specifically in the region related to the Gaussian energy. Furthermore, it has been established that the complexity of zero can be attained only at the complex RPA eigenenergy of the RPA density dipole mode within the Gaussian energy region.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, finance, and healthcare is a critical challenge. These systems are often represented as time-varying dynamic systems, where traditional clustering techniques based on static assumptions may not be effective. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for detecting clusters within dynamic systems in real-time by incorporating influence measurement into the embedding process. This method enables the identification of clusters that evolve over time and accounts for the interdependencies between system variables. We evaluate our approach using both synthetic data and real-world examples, including the New England electricity grid, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately tracking evolving clusters and providing robust results even in the presence of measurement errors.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task, as current text encoding methods struggle to capture the complex probability distribution of language. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach called SparseGAN, a novel GAN architecture for neural text generation. By incorporating the sparse max operator into the generative network and leveraging the vast vocabulary of language, SparseGAN effectively models the language distribution. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that SparseGAN outperforms the state-of-the-art generative models in terms of flow-based and bigram matching scores. Additionally, SparseGAN exhibits superior performance in terms of coherence and semantic similarity, outperforming even the strong baselines in terms of human-like quality.

The concept of interstellar pansomosis, which suggests that life could be transferred from one planet to another via interstellar space, is a fascinating yet controversial topic. To explore this idea more deeply, we used the radio spectroscopy technique to search for biological markers in the interstellar medium. Specifically, we looked for molecular phosphatidic acid, a fundamental building block of life on Earth, found in the T Tauri star system, Iota Forani, and the Vega star system. Our analysis revealed no definitive signs of the molecule in any of these systems. However, our instrument's ability to detect the molecule would have been sufficient had it been present in the Mars-like planets of those systems at concentrations comparable to those found on Earth. This study paves the way for a more rigorous application of radio spectroscopy in the search for extraterrestrial life.

Using the Interferometric HI intensity mapping 2D Power Spectrum Survey perturbation theory predictions are compared with N-body simulations to evaluate the accuracy of the former. Although the former can accurately describe the 1D power spectrum, it falls short in describing the 2D power spectrum, particularly on nonlinear scales. Although foreground removal techniques such as 2D Gaussian deconvolution and model subtraction techniques improve the accuracy of power spectrum estimates, they also introduce artificial features that affect the statistical distribution of the data.

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical model called ISSC. This model is mathematically equivalent to an $SU(N_f)$ gauge theory with $N_f$ massless fermions, semi-classically demonstrating sequential symmetry group reductions from $SU(N_f)$ to $U(1)^{N_f-1}$ via the formation of vacuum condensates. In contrast, quantum mechanically, the ISSC exhibits distinct characteristics from its classical counterpart, as quantum effects cause the vacuum to collapse into a single state breaking the symmetry to $U(N_f-1)$, with $U(N_f-1)$ being a proper subgroup of $U(N_f-2$, and so on. In the specific case of ISSC, quantum and classical beta functions exhibit the same properties of turning negative and then positive at distinct values.

Animal population studies often focus on understanding how animals interact with their environment and other species to promote effective conservation. A vital aspect of their habitat is the resource they depend on for survival. Our goal is to enhance statistical methods for analyzing space use by incorporating information about available resources. A new statistical model has been developed, which integrates resource selection data with spatial capture-recapture, taking into account the location of detected animals and the available resources in their environment. This integrated model allows researchers to simultaneously estimate animal movement patterns and their interaction with the environment, as well as make informed management decisions. A critical component of this model is a statistical framework for modeling the distribution of resources, which is essential for accurate analysis. The efficacy of the integrated model is demonstrated through analysis of data from a study on wild cats in the Kalahari Desert, and potential applications for this approach are discussed.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G$ and edge costs in $G$, with the objective of selecting an edge subset that satisfies certain connectivity requirements while minimizing total cost. A recent extension of this problem considers power edge costs and requires the selection of $k$ edge-disjoint subsets, with each subset meeting the connectivity requirements; minimizing total cost is achieved by minimizing the maximum cost among the subsets. For "obvious" instances where $k$-paths between specific nodes are required, we can approximate this problem with a factor of $2\xi(2k)^{2/3}$, with $\xi$ being the approximation ratio for the minimum number of edges in a basesize $2k$ system. Notably, this approach yields a $4$-approximation algorithm for the case when $k$-paths between $2k$ nodes are required.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding, Generalized 8-Player Normal Form Game (NFNFG), and Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) re-planning.

The concept of localization has long fascinated physicists and now finds applications in analyzing dynamic processes on complex networks. To study this, we have developed a novel metric called the participation ratio, which quantifies the spread of an excited state across the network nodes. By applying this tool to linear dynamics such as diffusion and synchronization on random networks, we discovered an unreported feature: the emergence of a distinct scale in participation ratio distributions. This characteristic scale signifies a boundary between two regimes: one where the dynamic is localized and another where it is delocalized. Notably, we discovered that a regime of weak delocalization is more prevalent in many network topologies, with localized dynamics occurring only as it becomes more extreme. Furthermore, we discovered that the emergence of weak and strong delocalization regimes can be attributed to competing node degree modes in network space, with intermediate modes promoting delocalization and extreme modes promoting localization.

This research focuses on assessing the effectiveness of a team's defensive strategy in football by calculating the likelihood of scoring against the opposing side. Specifically, it employs the concept of "generalized valuation of defense" (GVD) to analyze and rank teams' defensive capabilities. The study gathers data from official sources regarding the 2020 European Football Championship and compares its findings to results from the 2022 World Cup, utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation to model the influence of player positioning on the likelihood of scoring. A logistic regression model is then used to analyze how the GVD is affected by the location of the attacking and defending players. The outcome of this research reveals that the optimal positioning of a team's players can significantly impact the likelihood of scoring, thereby validating the efficacy of the GVD in evaluating the performance of football players and providing a valuable tool for coaches to refine player positioning and enhance their defensive capabilities.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method for identifying pre-printed text as either labels or content, despite the poor condition of the forms. Our approach uses a combination of a convolutional neural network and a set of template rules, where the neural network handles the extraction of intact text and the templates fill any missing links based on the connection of confirmed labels and fields. Our method has shown a significant reduction in errors compared to other layout-designer approaches on historical forms.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but a significant challenge exists when the underlying data dynamics shift. Traditional approaches use model ensembles, yet they incur high computational costs. In contrast, a single 'hidden parameter' can represent alternative models, providing a balance between a model that represents complex dynamics and one that represents a simple linear baseline. This approach enables efficient detection of changes in data dynamics and automatic selection of the hidden parameter through variational inference, thus achieving an optimal balance. We demonstrate our method, which can handle up to 100 dimensions, on both synthetic data and real-world applications like the S&P 500 index, showing its ability to adapt to changing data environments.

Independent unitary and Hermitian random matrices, subject to the same type of symmetry, exhibit similar behavior as large-N, and can be represented by specific symmetric polynomials, known as free convolution of type $B$, with determinantal structures.  This paper provides an in-depth examination of 'type $B$' freeness, a variant of standard freeness suitable for symmetric matrices, and offers a rigorous proof of 'type $B$' freeness for a broader category of unitary matrices.  Moreover, it investigates conditional freeness, a variant of standard freeness given certain conditions, and demonstrates that certain types of Hermitian random matrices, subject to the same type of symmetry, and conditioned to be positive definite, maintain analogous distributional behavior as large-N, and can be described by their unconstrained potential functions.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny.

Determining the extent of structural polarization within a society is a significant challenge in the analysis of social media and online communities. Polarization manifests through distinct communities forming within a network, which can be identified through the network's composition and how its members interact with one another. We examined multiple structural polarization metrics by testing them on randomly generated networks and real-world social media and scientific collaboration networks. The results showed that some of these metrics are heavily influenced by network density rather than polarization, and we developed a normalization procedure to standardize their values. This normalization involved comparing each metric to its expected value given a network's density, allowing the polarization-promoting metrics to be used as effective indicators of polarized network structures. The metric with the highest standardized value was found to be the betweenness-based Garamani index, which we suggest as a reliable measure of polarized network structures.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various systems where different interactions coexist between components, such as neurons, power grids, and oscillators that synchronize. To address the complexity of these networks consisting of two separate layers, researchers often apply symmetry assumptions, thus restricting analysis to specific types of "coupled" or "decoupled" solutions. This study investigates the synchronization properties of multilayer networks by exploring a model of two interconnected Kuramoto networks, and develops a method to analyze a broader class of solutions on these networks. It is discovered that there are multiple distinct solutions possible in these networks and that both the interlayer connections and structural features within each layer significantly impact them. Furthermore, evidence is found that certain configurations of network topology can facilitate or impede the emergence of multilayer solutions and that an inability to exchange information across layers can result in hysteresis effects that do not occur in single-layer networks.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant, is given. This framework is applied to the Cauchy stress operator, resulting in a characterization of equilibrium states as the compatibility conditions of first-order infinitesimal rigid body movements, the movement gradient being the compatibility matrix. Furthermore, the stress operator divides the space of symmetric square tensors at any point in a Lie algebra into two distinct subalgebras. One subalgebra comprises the stress operators generating the infinitesimal rigid body movements, and the other, larger subalgebra, is made up of the equilibrium states. Notably, this compatibility matrix has an associated algebra of endomorphisms, where some members operate on the equilibrium states, determining their equilibrium states compatibility operators and dividing the equilibrium states compatibility matrix endomorphisms into two parts. A comprehensive set of endomorphisms is characterized that yield equilibrium states from infinitesimal rigid body movements through the stress operator invariant relationship, and a minimum parametrization of the equilibrium states is determined as a function of the infinitesimal rigid body movements and their compatibility matrix.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide a robust framework for ensuring the reliability of software, with a focus on a geometrically based testing methodology that can be applied independently or in conjunction with verification. This approach is underpinned by a state-space graph that mirrors the design's underlying structure, which is generated automatically from source code and used to create a range of testing scenarios. These graphs can also be extended with additional edges representing possible ideal behavior, which can be explored during the testing process. Furthermore, the distribution of test inputs can be analyzed to identify design areas that are inadequately tested and may contain undetected bugs, which can be safely crashed into to pinpoint areas of concern.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts are generated dynamically by HyperNetworks given specific task inputs, enabling each task to have its unique processing style. The integration of hyper-prompts allows for enriched query representations, allowing for efficient information processing and optimization of model resources. The result is a more coherent and logical flow of information that enhances the model's ability to interpret and handle complex data.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$, $D_l$, or $E_l$, where $l$ is at least $3$. Let $V$ be the corresponding root system representation. By examining the Galois transformation $\sigma$ on the set of weights $\chi \in X(T)$ of a torus $T$, we investigate the effect of $\sigma$ on the orbits of weights under the Weyl group $W$. Specifically, we determine the length of the interval defined by adjacent weights related by $\sigma$, and this has implications for understanding the structure of representations of simple algebraic groups over finite fields.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model is preserved in the system's ground state, which exhibits the photon bundle emission parity following changes in the photon number state parity. Adding a small amount of anharmonicality to the cavity mode causes a shift to an odd-parity mixed state from which two photons are emitted preferentially, maintaining the parity symmetry in the emitted photons' number state. The protection of photon bundle emission by parity symmetry holds promise for creating protected quantum states and light sources in the ultrastrong coupling regime.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm capable of estimating a sparse, complex network's node count, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes (not exceeding the network's actual node count), where the estimated count is guaranteed to be accurate by a factor of two. The algorithm operates in a single, synchronized round and relies on the participation of a subset of the network's node population. Furthermore, the algorithm is node-efficient, necessitating the participation of only a sparse network's quadratic node count for precise estimation, significantly surpassing the best-known asynchronous algorithm's requirement of an attack node's cubic network size in the presence of an unlimited number of malicious nodes.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach calculates the connection variables directly from the physical fields, bypassing the need to solve the 4th order Hamiltonian constraint. Instead, it transforms the constraint into an equation for the logarithm of the conformal factor, which can be solved using standard methods. By setting the momentum connection variables to zero to satisfy the momentum constraints, the conformal factor is set to its average value. This technique is applicable to both scalar field models and realistic simulations involving neutron stars, as demonstrated in this study.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revived interest in this phenomenon. A particular class of materials, known as antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, has been identified as having exceptional anomalous Hall responses. This study delves into the anomalous Nernst effect in the same class of materials, specifically focusing on antiferromagnetic Mn$_3$NiN films. Our measurements revealed an anomalous Nernst effect that is orthogonal to the orientation of the net magnetization, and the anomalous Nernst coefficient achieved a remarkable magnitude of 55 $\mu$V/V/K at temperatures of 10K. Notably, the magnitude of this anomalous Nernst effect is 10 times greater than the ordinary Nernst effect in these films. Furthermore, by applying an in-plane electric field, we observed a significant reduction of the anomalous Nernst effect by 50%, indicating the potential for low-power control of this effect in antiperovskite materials.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted the field of natural language understanding. To create robust applications, a pre-trained model is usually necessary. However, training a single teacher model on a limited labeled dataset can result in a performance drop. In contrast, training multiple teacher models and averaging their outputs has been shown to enhance robustness. Unfortunately, averaging logits is constrained by the need to align dimensionality and doesn't leverage label information. To address this, we propose Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel approach that combines multi-teacher distillation with label information in an iterative, pairwise manner. Our method achieves better stability and accuracy than both the baseline and conventional single-teacher training, requiring no additional hyperparameters.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic.

User facilities like synchrotron radiation sources and X-ray free-electron lasers enable researchers to study a wide range of materials by rapidly collecting high-quality data. However, operating these machines and ensuring optimal performance of experimental tools present significant challenges. Users often lack the necessary background in accelerator physics and tool engineering to fully grasp the underlying processes. As a result, a new field has emerged, focusing on developing sophisticated instruments and software to facilitate easy access to these facilities' instruments. Despite numerous advances, there is still room for improvement in creating robust solutions that can handle the complexity of these tools. In this paper, a new approach is proposed, which emphasizes using a machine learning framework to streamline the process of developing such solutions. By incorporating a machine learning framework, it is now possible to rapidly prototype, test, and deploy a wide variety of machine learning models that can perform a range of tasks, including processing data in real-time, enhancing image quality, and predicting signals. This has led to the deployment of over 15 such models at two synchrotron facilities, enabling experimental tools to process data in real-time and achieve optimal performance automatically.

This paper aims to prove decay properties of the normalized gradient of a solution to a specific non-autonomous obstacle problem, defined by the equation min{u-f, au-a^D-u=0}, where the function u satisfies specific growth conditions. The decay result obtained here paves the way for establishing C^{1,alpha}-regularity of the obstacle domain in the aforementioned problem.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for effectively solving computationally demanding optimization problems, especially N-body problems that involve repulsive interactions between real and imaginary numbers. This often results in a first-order phase transition, which can be harnessed to achieve annealing time shorter than the computationally heavy second-order time. In this research, a critical observation was made - the sudden catastrophic failure of quantum annealing occurs when non-stoquastic Hamiltonians are employed, which arises due to the emergence of highly excited quantum states near the annealing endpoint. This issue arises frequently in practical N-body problems, in particular those utilizing plane waves to describe real, repulsing particles. A groundbreaking discovery indicates that stochastic behavior can be substituted with coherent behavior, enabling quantum annealing to function efficiently in the vicinity of the catastrophic failure point, achieving a significantly improved success rate and a annealing time that is two orders of magnitude faster than successful stoquastic quantum annealing.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1939 to 1944, during the mayoral tenure of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn in Groningen. The context of van Rhijn's term is discussed, with a focus on his background, the laboratory's planning process, and the implementation of Selected Areas. The author's analysis draws from the municipal archives of Groningen, the van Rhijn family archives, the archives of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, the University of Groningen's administrative archives, the University of Groningen's astronomical archives, the archives of the Groningen Municipal Library, the library's online resources, the library's astronomical library, and the library's onomastic archive.

We provide a detailed explanation of how certain central character properties and specific inertia actions on cohomology modules of GL_2-deformed rings lead to irreducible modules over these rings, thereby deforming classical Serre weights for GL_2.

We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a given compact set, under the condition that the solution's boundary has limited mean curvature. This achievement stems from an derivation of 'flatness' estimates for such hypersurfaces, characterized by a parameter reflecting the size of an optimal geometric component. These estimates, in turn, depend on earlier work on the flatness of minimal hypersurfaces. The results provide a foundational framework for the study of minimal and mean curvature optimized hypersurfaces.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for deeper neural networks. Research indicates that the proposed method exhibits enhanced stability and converges to an optimal solution when specific critic connections are established. Theoretical analysis supports the finding that only certain critic modules significantly impact convergence rates. Experimentation with main networks of varying depths demonstrates the method's performance, exhibiting improved convergence and output loss reduction compared to traditional sequential training.

Advanced composite materials have achieved significant damage control capabilities through self-sensing properties enabled by integrated fiber networks that facilitate real-time identification of structural integrity issues via electrical methods like EIT. While state-of-the-art shape reconstruction techniques like TV inversion are effective, their application to structural health monitoring is hindered by a lack of precise damage shape accuracy. This study explores the impact of varying grid sizes and node locations on the accuracy of identified structural defects using EIT, and introduces an alternative grid node allocation method to enhance reconstruction accuracy. A novel approach to grid node allocation is presented and applied to data obtained from embedded fiber networks, resulting in a highly effective shape reconstruction method that combines TV inversion with a modified node allocation strategy, known as TV-NAA. This approach allows for real-time data processing and produces accurate structural damage shapes, with validation conducted on a controlled lab experiment involving deliberate structural failures in EIT-infused composite panels.

We're exploring the concept of complexity, which, despite its widespread use, lacks a universally accepted definition. To shed light on this topic, we examine two distinct systems: the highly regulated flow of traffic at an uncontrolled intersection and the less regulated flow of ants foraging in a trail. By applying specific criteria for complexity, we aim to illustrate how simpler components can collectively create more complex systems, or vice versa, depending on the context.

We explore a control theory approach using lateral connections in neural networks, which enables learning policies that incorporate external information and prior knowledge. This framework utilizes optimal trajectory planning techniques, specifically Chattering-free Time-Optimal Control (CTOC), which can be applied to high-dimensional and nonlinear dynamical systems. By integrating CTOC with the learned policy through local feedback, the system achieves efficient use of computational resources and reduced training time. This method was successfully applied to a complex simulation that included multiple nonlinear robots navigating various environments, which demonstrated the ability to achieve diverse locomotion patterns using pre-trained walking gaits and a single training experience. Furthermore, the system was able to explore new states without additional training, which reduced the time required for convergence to under 1 second.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A new, extremely light scalar or pseudoscalar particle would ideally have been discovered already. Previous constraints would have been significantly improved if the particle had an unexpectedly long lifespan due to accidental symmetry, allowing it to travel vast distances before decaying. As a result, experiments designed for unstable particles like the Higgs boson should also have looked for highly energetic, collinear pairs that detach from each other after one particle decays into distant detectors. In this study, we propose using complementary approaches from flavor and astroparticle/dark matter physics to constrain non-baryonic dark matter or light exotic particles that interact weakly. We specifically study the effects of such particles on the flavor-changing process $K\to E^+E^-$, as well as on the stability of the dark baryon sector, and demonstrate how they could explain the anomaly in the $K^+K^-$ mass distribution without disrupting baryon anti-baryon symmetry.

This study explores the impact of remote learning on college students during the COVID-19 pandemic. Remote learning was found to have a significant negative effect on the ability of students to keep up with their coursework. Furthermore, remote learning had a substantial indirect effect on students' on-track status by influencing their academic performance. Notably, the results indicated that students who learned from home had a significant decline in on-track status due to remote learning.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as higher-collective descriptions of critical two-dimensional systems that can be represented by an infinite number of degrees of freedom. This paper focuses on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory and provides a detailed analysis of its symmetry properties, including an infinite set of conserved currents in a spectral parameter form. A step further is made in providing a collective description of the primary fields in terms of a set of elementary variables, which corresponds to a set of affine $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ currents. This analysis yields a collective description of the stress-energy tensor and reveals that the current algebra possesses additional relations that mirror the equations of motion. A similar set of equations can be derived for the elementary variables, which, when solved, offer a spectral collective description of the primary fields. This solution implies that the primary fields are related to certain eigenvalues of a matrix variable, which evolves according to the affine $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ equations of motion. A similar mechanism is also applied to the stress-energy tensor to obtain its secondary fields in terms of eigenvalues of a matrix variable, which relates to the Gelfand-Dickey hierarchy. A similar approach is taken to the conserved charges to show that they can be expressed as certain integrals of eigenvalues, which, when differentiated, result in an infinite set of charges consisting of Wronskians of eigenvalues. A similar mechanism is also applied to the Vir
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering, we found that multiple Killing horizons form as a result.  By analyzing the scattering in detail, it was also shown that, under certain conditions, the minimum charge-to-radius ratio of the resulting merger product can be achieved, thereby confirming the validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture. Furthermore, the analysis revealed a connection between the multiple Killing horizons and the surface areas of an event horizon and a cosmological horizon, which can be attributed to the near-extremal black hole's thermodynamic behavior and the near-horizon AdS geometry's influence on the AdS horizon's thermodynamic properties.

In this paper, we offer a novel, non-classical interpretation of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory by employing a four-valued logic system. By utilizing the paraconsistent and paracomplete logics LP~Q~, we adapt the ZF axioms to the weakened logic LP~Q~, and demonstrate that the resulting modified axioms, including the adjusted separation axiom, are sound within the framework of the two-valued model of classical Q-ZF.

Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have been driven by neural recording technology, allowing for more precise analysis of neural activity and improved decoding of user intentions. In a groundbreaking study, the team successfully recorded high-density electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals from the motor cortex in walking humans and interpreted the intended walking states and step rates of one participant. They trained an algorithm using L1 sparse regression to interpret the signals and found that it could accurately decode walking states with 95.83% precision and step rates with a correlation coefficient of 0.944. The results indicate a strong linear relationship between the algorithm's output and the actual step rates, achieving a correlation coefficient of 0.853. Notably, the study demonstrated for the first time that high-density ECoG signals can capture intricate patterns of step rate modulation during human locomotion. This discovery has significant implications for the future integration of BCI technology into active BCIs, which could one day assist users with gait disorders by providing precise control over walking movements.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution, another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling, and a final study on predicting outcomes in the FIFA World Cup using mutual information.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods have been successfully applied to analyze brain connectivity patterns, which are depicted as graphs where nodes symbolize brain areas and the edges between them represent the strength of connectivity. These graph representations are key to understanding how the brain functions. However, most traditional connectivity models overlook the fact that connectivity patterns are not static but change over time. In this study, we introduce a novel graph neural network model, DDEC, capable of estimating dynamic, directed connectivity matrices from time series data. By utilizing a customized variation of the Granger causality index, DDEC captures dynamic connectivity patterns and their evolution. Our approach is evaluated on both synthetic data and real-world fMRI scans, and the results show that it can accurately identify dynamic connectivity changes associated with working memory tasks.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the history of various species, enabling them to account for phenomena such as hybridization that phylogenetic trees cannot. Unfortunately, the random generation of phylogenetic trees is a common practice in their topological analysis, but there is no comparable method for phylogenetic networks due to their increased complexity. This complexity stems from the presence of reticulation cycles in their structure, which can vary in number and position, creating distinct components that must be maintained during the generation process. As a result, the study of random phylogenetic networks lacks the established foundation seen in the case of trees. A new set of network generation algorithms has been proposed to address this gap, which, although producing a computationally more expensive output, can be fine-tuned to prioritize computational efficiency. These algorithms are accompanied by the associated topological distribution codes for the resulting phylogenetic networks.

Animals move in diverse ways for survival, and understanding this behavior is crucial. Traditional methods of studying locomotion rely on manual annotation, which is subjective and time-consuming. We present a new, objective method for identifying and classifying biological motion automatically. This method can be applied to various video sources, including scientific datasets and naturalistic footage. We demonstrate our approach on two distinct datasets, walking and swimming fish.

The vast amount of data generated in modern science and its corresponding computational modeling has led to an increase in size and complexity of matrix systems that must be solved. As solving these systems becomes increasingly time-consuming, there is a critical need for efficient algorithms capable of rapidly solving large matrix systems. This paper presents an innovative algorithm that expedites the iterative inversion of matrix systems by leveraging a combination of higher order methods and sparse matrix operations, enabling the simultaneous update of all matrix elements. Notably, this new algorithm leverages the unique capabilities of GPU acceleration to take full advantage of the processing power available in modern hardware.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived expressions apply to both bounded and unbounded scattering environments.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. The transition between this phase and the disordered phase can be marked by the emergence of an extended state with a singular probability distribution. In contrast, the transition to a critical point involves an average of the winding number equal to 0.5, signifying the presence of a macroscopic localized state with an average occupation of 0.5.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield equivalent geometric frameworks, thereby supporting the concept that genus one curves possess an inherent, method-independent structure. The study also establishes new connections between the genus one curve and its associated elliptic elliptbox graph.

This paper delves into a comprehensive computation of the standard model Higgs boson production cross-section, accompanied by a pair of muons, in a specific supersymmetric standard model where the muon mass matrix includes complex components, allowing for on-shell Higgs production. Additionally, the on-shell process is compared to the off-shell Higgs process and a discussion of on-shell processes producing on-shell top quarks is included. Additionally, on-shell Higgs constraints on superpotential parameters are derived.

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's quasi-score linearity test statistic converges at the $O(n^{1/2})$ rate, which is a notable feature. The development of the test involved the use of randomization techniques for the null distribution of the on-sample rank-based score test, and its performance was evaluated through simulation experiments. Empirical results from an analysis of the 2010 US mayoral election data demonstrate the practical application of the test.

Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within neural networks, with the aim of enhancing their performance on various application problems. By incorporating advances in automatic differentiation, we can analyze specific examples in detail, focusing on inverse kinematics and blind inverse problems. Through this focused examination, we can identify the key characteristics of well-behaved differential mappings and explore methods to utilize the inherent structure of optimization problems in utilizing declarative networks more effectively.

A cell's behavior, movement, and the movement of proteins within a living organism are influenced by a cell's ability to spread and relocate proteins on the cell's outer membrane. This is because the cell's outer membrane is not static, but a dynamic surface that allows proteins to interact with one another. To better understand this complex process, a new computational framework is proposed to simulate adipocytes, a type of mammalian cell, by using the principles of fluid dynamics and the relocation of proteins on the cell's outer membrane. This framework is based on the assumption that proteins move freely across the cell's outer membrane, and that proteins can be subjected to various forces, such as the tendency of proteins to stick to one another, and the movement of the cell itself. To further refine this framework, the meshless moving-kernel technique is employed to model the interaction between proteins and the cell's outer membrane. This allows for a more accurate representation of the proteins' behavior, and the cell's movement, and the framework is validated by comparing the results to experimental data.

The unique properties of blockchain technology, such as its immutable and transparent nature, have made it an attractive platform for cryptocurrency transactions. Unfortunately, malicious actors have also taken advantage of the anonymity provided by cryptocurrency transactions to engage in illegal activities. Although on-chain analysis tools exist to examine the transaction history within a blockchain, they often lack interpretability and are not designed to visualize complex money trails. Existing methods typically focus on identifying illegal actors and do not provide a comprehensive analysis of the transaction patterns. In response to these limitations, we developed an interactive visualization system called CAT that utilizes attribute graphs to visualize and analyze money trails within a blockchain. This system enables users to track the flow of funds, explore transaction patterns, and gain a deeper understanding of the intricacies of money trails. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by utilizing it to investigate the money trails associated with the Bitcoin King and the Ethereum DAO hack incidents.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deep Q-learning as an example, we successfully created a rapid flit-based decoder capable of handling simultaneous multi-flip faults in its environment testings, showing promising results compared to commonly used classical flare-based algorithms and tools. Furthermore, this approach allows for tailored development of decoding methods specific to individual electronic error correction code instances, potentially eliminating the need for the complex and resource-intensive flipping procedures.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished by formulating interference patterns based on different paths taken by quantum particles. The use of quantum particles' sensitivity to infinitesimal changes in their environment allows for highly sensitive measurements. This paper investigates the effects of a particle's two-cavity on interference patterns and their sensitivity. It is shown that specific quantum states, when subjected to a single interaction with a two-cavity and a single external level, can achieve a Heisenberg-limit sensitivity. The study also examines the role of quantum jumps in identifying cavity occupations through interference patterns and investigates the role of the external level's coupling strength in enhancing interference patterns and Heisenberg-limit sensitivity. It is found that maximum Heisenberg-limit sensitivity occurs when the quantum jump probability of the two cavities' occupations is maximized.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2010. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased production, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess is more pronounced for hadrons with low transverse momentum, especially in association with direct photons. Additionally, the average hadron momentum is increased in the cold nucleus in $d$$+$Au collisions. These observations are supported by various theoretical models.

This paper explores the behavior of Smarandache's sequence from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) at A061076, specifically focusing on its associated sequences A061077 and A061078, which represent thesm(n), or the product of the digit sums of n when iteratively applied, under general conditions. We generalize existing results and provide evidence that the sequence sm(n) is highly composite, indicating that sm(n) often possesses a multitude of divisors.

Cloud-based HPC deployments leverage public and private clouds for increased flexibility and cost-effectiveness. Although these deployments offer significant advantages, high network variability can introduce unpredictable performance and cost implications. This study investigates the HPC-relevant aspects of public cloud network variability, focusing on its H-shape influence on application scalability from both performance and cost perspectives. We developed a flexible analytical model to simulate diverse application behaviors under varying network conditions. Using real-world data, we tested the model's accuracy. The results indicate that noise can lead to substantial changes in application cost and end-user experience, with impact severity depending on application scale. We further discovered that certain applications can achieve better scalability by being deployed as smaller, multiple instances rather than a single large instance.

In this paper, we investigate the setting where multiple learners, isolated from
one another and unaware of the others' existence, learn separately in
disconnected contextual linear bandit environments.
We consider a group of $G$ learners that have been learning for a total of $n$
context presentations in a context that is presented regularly.
We propose a novel algorithm which allows these $G$ learners to adapt to their
local contexts and at the same time take advantage of the knowledge that is
being acquired by others.
We show that this algorithm results in an context-specific regret of $O(n^{2/3}n^{1/6}\sqrt{d}\sqrt{d})$ and a regret of $O(n^{2/3}(d\sqrt{d})^{1/6})$ and which is
