This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two distinct fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the model's capacity for explicit solution, we examine a scenario where the swimmer moves along a line and a scenario confined to a flat surface. Notably, in both instances, the most effective strategy involves swapping the swimmer's environment exactly once, and we also investigate the impact of the fluid's properties and the swimmer's configuration on the efficiency of its movement.

Urban settings are known to be socially and economically diverse and can inspire innovative ideas through social learning. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, reduced face-to-face interaction due to lockdowns and distancing measures may have impacted the diversity of urban social engagement and consequently social diversity learning. By using mobile data from 12 US cities spanning the pandemic period, we assessed how social contact diversity changed. Our analysis revealed a significant decline in the diversity of urban encounters during the pandemic, with the effect being more pronounced in larger cities. This was linked to lower urbanization levels and increased adherence to pandemic guidelines. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the reduction in diverse face-to-face interaction led to a significant decrease in the socioeconomic diversity of urban encounters, with people living in less diverse neighborhoods during the pandemic having lower education levels on average. This study suggests that decreased diversity of face-to-face interaction may have broader implications for the social diversity learning process in urban areas.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding accretion disks are prone to episodic accretion and disk-star mergers in the early stages of their formation. A key factor in this process is the growth of spiral arms in regions of low viscosity, which can cause mass in the inner disk to fall onto the star in periodic bursts. When mass builds up above approximately ten solar masses in the inner disk, a disk-star merger occurs, releasing a mass of about one solar mass onto the star in a short period. These large fluctuations in mass can be attributed to the balance between accretion and merger events and have a significant impact on the development of the star, including its surface temperature, luminosity, and chemical composition. As such, episodic accretion and mergers should be factored in when modeling the evolution and properties of high-mass stars.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets in conformally invariant $\mathbb R_+^{+}$ in chiral RCFT without exotic elements. Furthermore, we've successfully retrieve the Buchholz-Kr\"uger-W\"ohrman interacting net and an example of a wedge-local non-type-III$_1$ net from Buchholz's scattering input. Using both Euclidean and operator-algebraic techniques, we obtain the same result.

The substantial adoption of 5G technology will soon be evident, and understanding children's exposure to it is crucial from both health and developmental perspectives. This study aims to assess how much 5G exposure children, schools, and hospitals experience in selected major US cities by analyzing near-field power density in 5G frequency bands. A near-field model based on 5G tower characteristics, taking into account 5G signal direction and power, is employed to estimate exposure levels. By utilizing this approach, a dataset of 5G towers in Alameda, Los Angeles, Miami, and New York has been created, and it is used to determine how much 5G exposure is experienced by children, schools, and hospitals in these areas. It is also investigated how the situation changes when 5G towers are added to Alameda and Los Angeles areas. Our analysis reveals substantial 5G exposure in Alameda, Los Angeles, Miami, and Miami, but notably less in New York, and adding more 5G towers in Alameda and Los Angeles increases exposure levels in these areas by 15% and 10%, respectively.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of three-dimensional water waves, specifically the waves' surface dynamics and volume dynamics, in the absence of any depth restrictions. Our analysis reveals that weak, long waves with constant vorticity cores exhibit linear growth rates in both surfaces and interior, in contrast to linear growth rates in vorticity and exponential growth rates in mixed vorticity fields. Our findings also indicate that nonlinear interactions between wave components in mixed vorticity fields occur at second order, in contrast to third order in uniform vorticity fields. A Hamiltonian Dysthe equation in two variables is developed to describe the evolution of a two-component wave envelope in mixed vorticity fields, in contrast to a one-variable wave envelope in uniform vorticity fields.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in urban environments poses significant challenges due to dynamic obstacles and complex road patterns. This paper presents a real-time, layered navigation controller for indoor navigation based on sonar data, capable of handling both simple and complex scenarios. The proposed system processes multiple sonar inputs to create a basic map of the surroundings and identifies the path to follow. It then applies a layered control approach to navigate along that path, avoiding collisions in real-time. A key feature of this controller is its ability to generate a virtual wall in the environment, guiding the robot towards the target while avoiding obstacles. Experimental results from various tests in different indoor settings demonstrate the controller's effectiveness in achieving smooth, real-time navigation. A significant outcome of these tests was the discovery of an optimal gain set for the virtual force, which was found to outperform methods used in other research studies in terms of both efficiency and ease of implementation.

The prevalence of false news on social media poses a significant problem,
especially for younger individuals who may lack the critical thinking skills
to differentiate between fact and fiction. One method of identifying false
information is by comparing multiple sources reporting on the same event.
However, this task can be quite demanding for users on social media platforms.
Our goal is to leverage the ability of automatic text summarization tools to
create a concise overview of an article's content and compare it to existing
fact-based data. By doing so, we can develop a more effective classifier to
distinguish between genuine and fabricated news stories.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these random fields – the geometry of their domain, particularly the curvature of the surface they reside on. The curvature influence is explored through statistical methods and theoretical derivations, showing how it alters the likelihood of events occurring within these random fields. The findings are supported through the development of step-by-step mathematical steps and demonstrated in a practical application involving the statistical analysis of the Galaxy Distribution in the universe. The results suggest that the curvature effect can be estimated and has significant implications for the understanding of the Galaxy Distribution. The research also suggests that the curvature effect can be estimated and has important implications for the understanding of the Universe's overall geometry. The results are derived through the use of sophisticated mathematical methods and are supported through the use of statistical evidence. The study contributes to the broader understanding of the Galaxy Distribution and the Universe's overall geometry. This research targets resolving security concerns for users in nonorthogonal multiple access systems by analyzing secure communication capabilities in a scenario where the base station's decoding order is unknown to the users. We examine the achievable secure communications in a one-user nonorthogonal multiple access system and uncover a connection between decoding order and secure communication rates. A key finding indicates that in the optimal secure communication scenario, the higher power user should be decoded first. Furthermore, a novel technique is introduced to solve the nonconvex optimization problem of determining the user decoding order using a low-complexity method, and it is proved that this approach yields an optimal solution. We also extend the analysis to a two-user scenario and offer an insightful user decoding order formula. Specifically, under certain conditions, it is possible to deduce the optimal user decoding order directly without solving complex optimization problems.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to high-dimensional data sets, it's common for the data dimensions to hinder efficiency. Dimensionality reduction techniques are designed to mitigate this issue by generating a smaller set of new coordinates that capture the essential information from the original data set. Specifically, this paper addresses the challenge of finding an optimal set of coordinates by minimizing a loss function that measures the difference between the original data and a projected data set consisting of fewer coordinates. Although the convex optimization framework is typically preferred for such problems, previous studies have shown that optimizing non-convex objectives can lead to more efficient solutions by enabling the discovery of solutions that are invariant to rotations. This paper presents an algorithm based on approximate fixed point computation that converges linearly to a solution that is stable under rotation, using an $\ell_1$ loss function. Numerical experiments indicate that this approach outperforms gradient descent methods by yielding higher accuracy and greater invariance to rotational transformations.

Recently, pre-trained language models like BERT have significantly
  accomplished various natural language processing tasks. However, training
  these models demands substantial annotated data, making the annotation
  process time-consuming and costly. In particular, annotating semantic roles
  in questions with emotional intent has proved especially challenging due to
  the complexity of analyzing who, what, and which aspects evoke emotions in
  questions. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced to refine the
  emotion-related question annotations by combining BERT's linguistic
  understanding with domain expert knowledge, effectively leveraging domain
  expert input to correct annotations in a more efficient and cost-effective
  manner. Furthermore, the benefit of employing semantic role annotations in
  training question classification is demonstrated through the proposed
  ABERT-QC framework, which incorporates annotations to refine the emotional
  questions' categorization via semantic role guidance and fine-tuning.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski previously enhanced the duality between finite and totally ordered groups by extending Friederica Shwartz and Daniel Scullard's energy lemma to cover totally ordered groups. Building on this, we demonstrate that certain properties of finite groups can be analogously applied to totally ordered groups, specifically those related to the "energy" concept. Our work expands on this by introducing a meaningful definition of energy for totally ordered groups and proving that a group with bounded energy is cyclic.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly and without a pattern, from that of the accretion disk's average spin. The identification of asynchronous polars among the general polar population is achieved by detecting asynchronous emission patterns through spectroscopic observations. Despite being defined as magnetic polars, many asynchronous polars exhibit notable X-ray hardness, with their X-ray spectra divided into distinct soft and hard components. In contrast, standard non-asynchronous polars display consistently soft X-ray spectra. This study delves deeper into the behavior of asynchronous polars, particularly in comparison to their non-asynchronous counterparts, by conducting detailed time-series analysis of their X-ray data. It reveals that a substantial majority of asynchronous polars exhibit emission patterns that vary between soft and hard states, while non-asynchronous polars consistently maintain their spectral profiles. Furthermore, it reveals that the majority of asynchronous polars possess short white dwarf spin periods below one second, with most exhibiting extremely powerful magnetic fields exceeding 10^11 Gauss. As such, it proposes that the classification of asynchronous vs non-asynchronous polars may be a result of competing forces between magnetic and centrifugal forces, influencing the behavior of the white dwarf's magnetic field and thereby affecting the characteristics of X-rays observed.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, a coupled method, and a loosely coupled (Ale-FI) technique. Additionally, this project aims to introduce the necessary tools for employing the Reduced Basis Method in fluid dynamics and structure dynamics, before delving into the more complex fluid-structure interaction scenario.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an accurate map of the environment is crucial. Creating a comprehensive and abstract representation of a space from a limited set of sensory data is a complex task. In this study, a novel topological map framework named HiTMap is introduced, allowing a robot to construct an accurate map of an unknown environment. HiTMap consists of a ring-shaped outer boundary, a series of radial lines, a central node, and corridor modules that form the map. The mapping process is broken down into three main components: identifying the outer boundary, determining the radial lines, and assembling the corridor modules. Furthermore, a succinct mathematical description of the environment is achieved through the collaborative input of real-world sensory data, facilitating an accurate and user-friendly map of the unknown space.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task detected offensive language in social media posts. For the development and evaluation phases, the team employed two separate classifiers: an initial linear one based on Izbas's baseline, often called "2nd generation", and a more advanced version using BERT, often referred to as "3rd generation". The BERT-based classifier matched the top-performing entry in its evaluation category, while both systems utilized the same features, allowing for a fair comparison. Notably, even the basic linear version outclassed many previous submissions by a significant margin. Consequently, the BERT version was created to further enhance performance. Another distinct aspect of this project was its focus on identifying the target of the offense, typically the author, and attempting to distinguish between them. Unfortunately, target detection proved challenging, especially given the limited available data for training. As such, only the BERT-based system was adapted for this task, incorporating an additional layer and trained with a small, carefully selected set of target indicators, often referred to as "slurs".

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields. This task is complicated by the need to differentiate between magnetic fields generated by mass and those generated by charge. A new method has been proposed to overcome this challenge by leveraging atomic interferometry and taking advantage of Meissner effect. This approach enables atomic interferometry to sensitively detect local magnetic field changes within a region affected by a superconductor's Meissner effect. A theoretical model predicts that a group of ~100 atoms can detect local magnetic field changes as minute as 10^-14 Hz^-1/2 at 1s measurement duration, which is 10 times more sensitive than the best current magnetometer using superconducting quantum interference. This enhanced sensitivity is due to the extreme values of atomic magnetic moments in comparison to those of electron spins.

We investigate the spin and thermal characteristics of a three-layered ferromagnetic insulator situated between two transition metal dichalcogenide systems using non-equilibrium Green's function methods enhanced by self-consistent scattering matrix techniques. Applying nonequilibrium self-consistent techniques, we discover that proximity effects cause magnetic polarization at both edges of the sandwich structure, and for an antiferromagnetic orientation, these induced moments cancel each other out in the central layer. Notably, the spin-dependent thermal conductance in the central layer exhibits a peak when the central TMDC layer is ferromagnetically oriented, and this value is four times higher than in the antimagnetic configuration.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. Two distinct cases are considered: a straight interface and a narrow gap, in both scenarios the electron spillover is examined as it approaches zero. In the straight interface case, we confirm that a finite parameter is necessary to obtain a meaningful result, reflecting additional energy the spillover induces. Conversely, in a narrow gap, the result is meaningful in the limit of zero spillover, in contrast to earlier studies on retardation effects which require very small gaps. We also analyze the resulting energy losses photons cause in the metal in both scenarios.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities and the distinct approaches of the different methods, which were initially introduced in 1993 and most recently in 2015.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the density matrix renormalization group, verifying results with exact diagonalization, and understanding these findings through green's functions and numerical analysis.

In the case of a finite admixture model where adherence to a specific direction is required, we have discovered a precise mathematical relationship with stochastic geometry and convex analysis. This allows us to characterize a particular additive measure as well as determine its associated concave function. Additionally, we have obtained a fundamental equation that directly links the additive measure to the concave function. If the condition of directionality is removed, this result can be used to provide a direct characterization of the Ferguson-Perkins-Walsh theorem.

Utilizing the method of Borel resummation, we have been able to derive the complete set of real anomalous dimensions associated with a specific class of twist-two operators in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, it is shown that traditional perturbation theory can only be viewed as the real component of complex anomalous dimensions. A new set of equations has been proposed that can accurately model both the magnitude and phase of anomalous dimensions, in addition to their perturbation theory components. Borel-resummed perturbation theory can be related to physical aspects of worldsheet strings moving through supergravity modes. A proposal is made that two-loop supergravity solutions can be depicted by classical strings moving through supergravity modes, in accordance with the boundary supergravity data.

High-performance computing on the GPU is being widely adopted in various fields, including scientific simulations, due to its ability to process complex computations efficiently. However, developing software that utilizes GPU effectively is often hindered by limited memory management capabilities in CUDA, which lacks a dynamic memory manager that can handle memory allocation, deallocation, and pointer management in a memory-safe manner. Existing memory allocators are typically optimized for specific applications, lacking the necessary support for common object-oriented features such as garbage collection and memory pooling. In this paper, we introduce a novel dynamic memory manager called DynaSOAr, designed specifically for GPU-based object-oriented programming. It provides a robust and flexible framework for memory allocation and deallocation, enabling developers to create more intuitive and effective GPU applications. A case study demonstrating the potential of DynaSOAr in fluid dynamics simulation is also presented, along with an analysis of its performance and efficiency.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the associated commutators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to model magnetic adatoms and clusters on superconducting surfaces, and this theory is applied to investigate Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states formed by Mn adatoms and pairs of Mn atoms on the Nb(110) surface. Utilising the theoretical framework, the surface YSR states are described from first principles in terms of the electron-hybridisation and the spin-polarisation of the underlying bulk electrons, and this description enables the spin-polarisation to be accurately calculated. The spin-polarisation of YSR states is in good agreement with experimental measurements found in literature, and the spin asymmetry of the YSR states is also explored. Notably, the spin asymmetry varies significantly as a function of energy and electron-hybridisation, and this mechanism may offer a viable path for manipulating electron flow in superconducting tunnel junctions through electrical means.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create an instance segmentation framework. FourierMask utilizes the Fourier series to map positions in the Fourier domain, enabling the implicit neural network to identify object instances based on fourier coordinates. This approach allows FourierMask to pinpoint instances with remarkable accuracy, often outperforming methods that rely on input 3D coordinates. Additionally, our model is capable of handling objects with discontinuous surfaces and can also identify multiple instances, albeit to a lesser extent. Despite using a limited number of input coordinates where three-dimensional coordinates are invalid, FourierMask exhibits extraordinary accuracy in instance segmentation.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using the Multi-angle Imager for Measuring Atmospheric Composition (MISR) and MODIS often fail within the veiled core of convective clouds with active updrafts. As a result, biases of one order of magnitude or more are produced in the retrieved values. This study investigates whether the combination of MISR and MODIS data can improve the retrieval process within the veiled core. A method is developed to identify the veiled core using a combination of the normalized difference veiling factor and updraft intensity factor. This method is applied to a dataset of 10.9 million cloud pixels from the MISR-MODIS joint product between 2002 and 2018. Characteristics of clouds with active updrafts and a prominent veiled core are identified. A method is presented to distinguish these clouds from those with inactive updrafts and a less prominent veiled core. An analysis of the scattering angle distribution within clouds with active updrafts and a prominent veiled core reveals a bimodal distribution, indicating a two-component cloud microphysical structure. In contrast, clouds with inactive updrafts and a less prominent veiled core exhibit a unimodal distribution. A method is presented to distinguish these two types of clouds using a statistical metric. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts an electron plasma, 
resulting in a series of white dwarfs and facilitating the acceleration of ions through a 
transparency barrier in the plasma. Under specific conditions where the laser frequency 
decreases over time, we observed significant ion acceleration, producing an energy 
distribution that follows a power law. This effect can be highly efficient in 
converting the energy of the laser into the kinetic energy of the ions, especially 
when the frequency of the laser decreases rapidly. This mechanism offers a simple 
explanation for the ion acceleration seen in experiments involving high-intensity 
chirped lasers and plasma targets.

The space telescope TESS has been pivotal in finding numerous planetary systems, some of which are still in their formation phase. Researchers used ground-based telescopes to find three additional planets around the TOI-712 star using transit spectroscopy and radial velocity methods. With a spectral type of K7 and a temperature of 3181 K, TOI-712 is one of the coldest stars with confirmed exoplanets. The four planets discovered orbit the star with periods ranging from 6.6 to 12.5 days. Although these planets are too far from their host star to support life, their masses are close to the boundary between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes. If a fifth planet were to exist within the habitable zone, it too would likely be a mini-Neptune rather than a rocky world. The formation of TOI-712 b and c may have been influenced by the migration of planets through the stellar disk, and further study of this system could provide valuable insights into how such systems develop.

This paper presents first-principles calculations of the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within carbon dioxide in a rutile structure, utilizing the ruRuSDP-CCSD(T) method of coupled cluster theory with DFT. Carbon and nitrogen defects were found to create localized states within the material's band gap. Specifically, carbon defects resulted in an n-type semiconducting material, while nitrogen defects led to a p-type semiconducting material. Carbon defects also caused an indirect to direct band gap transition, in contrast to nitrogen defects which maintained direct material characteristics. Furthermore, carbon defects maintained the material's overall stability, in contrast to nitrogen defects which caused distortions to the material's lattice structure.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, the proposed method is found to be insensitive to the accuracy of modeling final-state radiation. Using a dataset of 100 picobarns of data, no instances consistent with the top-quark fully elastic process are seen. No instances consistent with the semi-elastic process are found in three distinct searches, with maximum signal strengths of 0.48, 0.17, and 1.04 times the expected background at 95% confidence level. The ability to exclude certain processes based on the emitted quark-jet is demonstrated.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays have been instrumental in revealing the temperature fluctuations that occur at the scales of 10 to 100 kiloparsecs. These structure functions are typically analyzed using X-ray data obtained from spectral analysis of individual spatial bins. However, due to limited spatial resolution of current X-ray telescopes, measurements of these structures are often limited by statistical uncertainties. This study develops a framework to quantify the uncertainties that affect the reliability of current and future X-ray imaging-clustering measurements, specifically focusing on the impact of deconvolution of the instrument's point spread function. Moreover, it explores how next-generation X-ray instruments, with their improved capabilities for spectral and spatial analysis, will impact the accuracy of these measurements. The findings of this study are then applied to present data on the intra-cluster medium derived from the observations made by the Planck satellite and the XMM-Newton archive.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems in Ramsey theory and proposed the study of $\delta$ problems for various graph parameters. Specifically, they examined the Ramsey property of infinite graphs and defined $ram(\mathcal{G})$ as the smallest value of $ram(G)$ across all instances $G$ within the isomorphism class $\mathcal{G}$. In 2000, Erdos and Galvin proved that $ram(K_3\text{-colourable } 3\text{-regular graphs}) = 8/25$. In this study, we establish $ram(\mathbb{Q}^*-edges) = 1/4$, which is the optimal lower bound for $\gamma(ram(\mathbb{Q}^*-edges))$. In 1999, Preiss and Su provided a lower bound of 9/40. In 2002, Preiss offered an optimal construction for the upper bound of $ram(K_3\text{-colourable } 3\text{-regular graphs})$. Owing to the distinct nature of Preiss's construction from $\mathbb{Q}^*$, our result is $\mathbb{Q}^*$-based and thus differs from his work.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-shaped area with an anisotropic gas density structure. To investigate the 2D spatial characteristics of this region, researchers utilized the 2D spatial correlation function, a widely-used metric in various spatial science fields. The study revealed the typical 2D spatial scale associated with anisotropic density structures in the CMZ to be approximately 200 parsecs, a finding corroborated by multiple observational datasets, including continuum, dust emission, and CO observations. The research also displayed the long-tailed spatial distribution patterns of these structures on an anisotropic log-log graph. To better understand the 3D spatial characteristics of these density structures, a method was developed to convert the 2D correlation function and the results showed a typical 3D spatial scale of approximately 100 parsecs. The research indicates the complex, multi-scale spatial structure of these density structures in the CMZ, a feature observed in many other molecular clouds throughout the galaxy. The study suggests that the complex spatial configuration of these structures may pose a significant hindrance to star formation processes within the region.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method for identifying Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We observe that individuals suffering from Bell's Palsy exhibit an asymmetrical closure of their eyes, which can be seen as distinct facial features. Our proposed solution leverages these eye-focused characteristics to achieve accurate detection. By employing pre-trained models for face and eye recognition, we successfully reduced the size of our dataset to only include eye-focused bounding boxes. Through extensive experiments, our method demonstrated superior performance compared to existing approaches, with a notable improvement in F1 score of 0.1111. Furthermore, our data indicates a slower average closure time of eyes affected by Bell's Palsy, with a 0.0454 difference in seconds.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings show that simulations utilizing qutrits handle higher levels of noise better than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass gap values. Due to the phenomenon known as "correlator floor," where the correlator value converges to a certain value under high levels of noise, obtaining accurate results may require employing iterative reconstruction techniques to compensate for the introduced noise.

Our simulations and experimental setups combine high-intensity laser interactions with solid-density tin foil targets to produce dense, spin-polarized positron sources. When these targets are hit by a high-power, high-frequency linearly polarized laser, we find that spin-polarized positrons can be generated in abundance from magnetic fields within the targets. These fields are created by the interaction of the laser's high frequencies with the targets' plasma currents. A theoretical model based on the Breit-Wheeler-Born approximation demonstrates that the resulting positrons are predominantly spin-polarized due to their association with highly linearly polarized photons. As a direct consequence, a substantial degree of spin polarization is observed in the generated positrons. Furthermore, we propose a method to collect these positrons using a magnetic field generated by the same high-frequency interaction. This field not only traps the positively charged particles but also minimizes the required magnetic field to a range of 0.1 to 1 Tesla.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully integrated CMOS temperature sensor capable of continuous temperature monitoring. The proposed sensor is based on a bandgap-based sub-circuit that generates three distinct voltages in response to varying temperatures. An introduced method calculates the absolute temperature from these generated voltages. The designed sensor is compatible with a wide 0.6V to 1.8V 18-bit ADC supply range and demonstrates an inaccuracy of 1.4°C and a resolution of 0.24°C across temperatures between -40°C and 85°C. The sensor's low-power design results in 1.4nW, 0.65nW, and 0.24nW power consumption at supply voltages of 0.6V, 1.2V, and 1.8V, respectively. The chip's 52μm^2 area integrates a conversion circuit capable of achieving 1.06nJ and 4.06nJ energy per conversion without and with a 10x slowed-down process, resulting in compatible outcomes with the state-of-the-art solutions.

The long-standing enigma of rapidly rotating young stellar objects maintaining magnetic fields of over 1 kilogauss is scrutinized here. Various theories proposing magnetic field generation through stellar surface dynamics have been found wanting due to magnetic field dissipation under such conditions. It has now been demonstrated that magnetic fields configured axially symmetrically can persist indefinitely under these conditions, specifically in the form of toroidal fields aligned with the star's rotation axis of symmetry. The theoretical model of magnetic field generation in stellar surfaces is now compared with this axisymmetric stability model to yield the desirable conclusion that sufficiently strong magnetic fields will survive the stellar surface dynamics and rotate with the star as a whole.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse graining changes. A key question arises: can we derive a precise and universally applicable flow equation that accurately describes the system's evolution? To address this, the paper discusses testing hypothetical frameworks by comparing their predictions to numerical data and examining how different approaches, such as patching schemes, impact the results. The authors argue that due to the complexity of solving exact flow equations, a more practical method is needed and that due to its simplicity and broad applicability, the set of flow equations should be analyzed using numerical techniques. As a starting point, the paper examines one-dimensional quantum mechanics and field theories that exhibit $U(1)$ or $O(N)$ symmetries in zero-dimensional space, specifically studying the dynamics of set of flow equations for these models.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on exploring various geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks. Various cohomological concepts, including Hodge, de Rham, and Serre theories, are investigated within the framework of Lie groupoids and stacks. The research also aims to extend serre theories to the domain of differentiable stacks. Moreover, geometric constructs, such as connections, foliations, and characteristic classes, are examined on Lie groupoids and stacks, while a specific connection is analyzed in the context of a C^infty-stack of Riemannian manifolds.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows and those that are not.  Radio observations at 8.6 GHz show a significant core mass difference, with flowed cores associated with 1.3 mm sources being nearly twice as massive (0.19 M_sun) as non-flowed cores (0.10 M_sun).  Additionally, an examination of core excitation temperatures using 13CO and 13CO self-absorption spectra reveals no notable difference between non-flowed and flowed cores.  However, when comparing outflowing 1.3 mm sources to sources without outflows in 13CO line width, a 2 sigma difference of 0.35 km/s is found.  This difference is not evident in the derived 13CO self-absorption temperature difference.  The difference in line widths may be attributed to the low masses of the cores.  The results suggest that cores with outflows are beginning to gravitationally contract and could be on the verge of forming a massive star.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators and their corresponding relational semantics. Specifically, it examines the correspondence between the Tarski-Hesselbarth and Reiter theorems in this context, but with forest-representability instead of representability. Additionally, some results can be strengthened by adding axioms that restrict the associated forest algebras.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, enabling the development of machine learning models to make inferences about single LiDAR scans or integrate them with other types of data, such as images. This paper explores the application of machine learning to LiDAR data, highlighting key challenges and opportunities. We outline fundamental concepts for working with 3D point clouds and review the essential steps for preparing data for LiDAR learning tasks. A systematic overview of recent LiDAR learning algorithms is presented, covering classification, segmentation, object detection, and other relevant tasks. The discussion extends to multi-task and multi-modal learning, highlighting the current state of the field and potential areas for future research.

Recurrences in positive definite functions defined on the sphere have gained significant interest due to their applications in various fields, including the analysis of the CMB and other astronomical data. These recurrences can be initially expressed as the sum of a product of two functions and an irreducible component. Our research focuses on identifying pairs of spherical harmonics with the minimum degree difference that satisfy this condition for specific, commonly used stationary random fields. By analyzing the spherical harmonic expansion of these functions, we can determine the minimum degree of their irreducible component. Doing so allows us to establish recurrences for the Spherical Modified Bessel functions, Spherical Hankel functions, and the random fields themselves.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for over half a century. To shed light on this issue, researchers are correlating UHECRs with neutrinos at the Pierre Auger Observatory using data from both observatories. By cross-referencing 14.6 UHECR arrivals that may have originated from neutrino interactions with those directed away from known neutrino sources in the IceCube catalog, a bias towards source directions is found only at statistically insignificant levels. This study also explores additional methods to combine information from both datasets to enhance the correlation search, such as incorporating information from large-scale structures in the universe and the positions of active galactic nuclei within 300 megaparsecs. Similar to the single-neutrutrino analysis, no evidence of clustering around these two large-scale sources is found with probabilities of consistency with the null hypothesis of about 15% and 30%, respectively. The results from this study can be utilized to place constraints on cosmological models involving neutrino production mechanisms such as top-down models and decaying dark matter.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach of foam rheology and interface roughness theory, we investigate the frictional properties of Newtonian foams within 55 μm and 1.1 mm wide channels. By measuring the pressure drop across channels with varying widths and surface roughness, we find that the friction is surface roughness-dependent and remains constant, unrelated to foam viscosity. When the liquid volume fraction is close to the maximum, the foams exhibit solid-like behavior and follow the yield stress model. By comparing maximum sustainable pressures in narrow channels, we estimate yield stress, which is found to be surface roughness-independent. However, yield stress is foam viscosity-dependent. Our findings suggest that yield stress is directly proportional to the square root of maximum sustainable pressures in narrow channels, with the proportionality constant being surface roughness-specific. This research provides a method to determine the yield stress of maximum jammed foams using their interface roughness properties.

This report examines 20,000 images categorized into 6 distinct classes,
depicting normal skin and 5 types of skin cancer (melanoma, basal cell
carcinoma, actinic keratosis, benign nevus, and psoriasis). Initially, we
evaluated several classification methods, employing both feature extraction
techniques (VGG19, ResNet50) and a direct image-to-class approach (End-to-End)
using a small set of 2,000 images. Consequently, a hybrid model was developed,
utilizing features extracted by VGG19 and ResNet50, along with an image-to-class
method. Unfortunately, accurate cancer detection proved challenging due to
the presence of mislabeled outlier samples within the normal skin category.
To address this issue, we introduced a novel method that leverages decision
surface analysis and entropy calculation. This technique enables the
identification of mislabeled samples and their reassignment to appropriate
classes.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an infinitely elastic membrane.  A rotating setup facilitates the development of complex finger patterns at the membrane's point of maximum curvature, providing a point of comparison to the non-rotating finger instability commonly observed in Hele-Shaw cells.
